bio.en: Nikita Bier is a consumer-app builder who has launched more chart-topping apps than almost anyone else, selling tbh to Facebook for over $30 million and Gas to Discord for many millions more with a tiny team.
bio.zh: Nikita Bier 是一位消费级应用高手，他打造并推向排行榜榜首的应用数量几乎无人能及：以超过 3000 万美元将 tbh 出售给 Facebook，又以数千万美元将 Gas 出售给 Discord，且全程只有极小的团队与极少的资金。

summary.en: Nikita shares hard-won tactics for building viral consumer apps, emphasizing that you should hunt for latent demand where users jump through hoops to get value. He explains why building for teens (13-18) is the smartest wedge because their invitation rates collapse with age, and why most founders underestimate the chaotic grind of keeping a hit online. The conversation also covers how to recognize when to pivot and why product lives and dies in the pixels, not in documents.
summary.zh: Nikita 分享了打造病毒式消费应用的实战策略，强调要寻找用户愿意“绕远路”也要获得价值的潜在需求。他解释了为什么从青少年（13-18 岁）切入是最聪明的策略——因为随着年龄增长，用户的邀请率会骤降——以及为什么大多数创始人低估了维持一款爆款在线运转的混乱与艰辛。对话还涉及如何判断何时该转型，以及为什么产品的成败在于像素与体验，而非文档。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is insane. I did not know this full story.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A tip that you're sharing here is look for latent demand

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Where people are trying to obtain a particular value and going through a very distortive process. If you can actually crystallize what their motivation is, you can have this kind of intense adoption.
turns.zh: 即人们试图获取某种特定价值，却经历着极度曲折的过程。如果你能真正厘清他们的动机，就能实现这种强劲的用户增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know you're actually a product manager at Facebook.
turns.zh: 我不知道你实际上是Facebook的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: The thing I didn't realize as a product manager in a large tech company is there is very little product management that you do. They're mainly just writing documents and then being the team secretary and running around getting approvals, but products live and die in the pixels. You should be designing the hierarchy, the pixels, the flows, everything. That's on you.
turns.zh: 作为大型科技公司的产品经理，我之前没有意识到，真正能做产品管理的工作其实很少。他们主要就是写文档、充当团队秘书、四处奔波获取批准，但产品是靠像素而生而死的。你应该负责设计层级结构、像素、流程等一切环节。这都是你的职责。

首先，我想聊聊大家可能不太了解的你早期经历。你的首款产品Politify与如今的业务方向截然不同，而Politify恰恰是我非常向往的项目。它能根据候选人对生活的影响，帮助用户决定投票给谁。你能否分享一下那段经历，以及为何转向消费级应用？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: When I was in college, I was really interested in this kind of thing that American voters do, which is they vote against their own financial self-interest, like people in New York and San Francisco vote for Democrats for higher taxes. People in Kansas vote for Republicans for low taxes and they make less money, and so fewer government benefits. I wanted to build this tool that would help communicate the financial impacts of these policy proposals of presidents. I built it in my last year of college and it was just a web app that we put out and it would calculate their tax proposals, the government benefits that they were proposing, and you would enter in your basic personal information, how many kids you have, your age. Then it would just tell you in dollars what the impact would be. It'd also tell you, we simulated those policies also against the tax returns of every zip code so you could see how it impacts your community. (00:07:40): We went super viral. I think very few people thought of politics that way and I think we got 4 million users on it during that season, during that election. It was just like a project that we raised some grant money for, but it ended up feeding into this company that we spun up and that was called Outline. Because we had a bunch of governments reach out to us asking, "Can you build this for our budget?" The governor of Massachusetts actually reached out and I flew out there to meet with them and that was going to be our first customer. We raised some money, we won a government contract and we joined Techstars, the accelerator. We got a contract in the pipeline with the Obama administration and then we got this contract and we started building it and the government shutdown happened in the middle of like, as we were building it and we had one of our contracts canceled. (00:08:51): I realized I actually really don't like selling software to governments and my core competency all along was making things that go viral on the internet. That was what we had built, not this policy simulation tool. We went to our investors and we said, "Look, this isn't actually what we're excited about doing anymore." We offered to give the money back and said, "We're going to be building consumer apps and here's a few ideas that we have." None of them took the money back. Then we spent the next four or five years building a variety of different kind of consumer apps. We had a few mild successes during the course of those four to five years. One of them was an app called Five Labs that ingested your Facebook posts and determine your personality based on the language you use. It used this exact same model that Cambridge Analytica used, and that was super viral. I think we had tens of millions of profiles in it and it went viral in like three days. (00:10:09): We raised some more money based off the success of that and we started focusing a lot more on mobile after that first app, Five Labs. We launched basically every type of app you can imagine. We launched mapping apps, chat apps, event meetup apps. Basically, every consumer app on mobile that you could think of. That actually helped us build a muscle to understand what people want and how to actually make things grow and how to test them. Over time, we started focusing more on teens. A lot of people ask why Silicon Valley is so fixated on building apps for teens. (00:10:55): One of the reasons is their habits are pretty malleable. As we get older, we get fixed into our habits of using certain communication products and we don't really adopt new things. Then the other thing that we discovered was that adults don't really invite people to new apps. We found that as a user got older from age 13 to 18, the number of people that they invite to an app just declines almost exponentially. Finally, and the most important thing is they see each other every day, and that is so critical. Consumer app developers sometimes say smokers are great for targeting an audience because they actually hang out serendipitously a lot outside of buildings. Not to say social apps are cigarettes, I don't really like that metaphor.
turns.zh:
读大学时，我对美国选民的行为深感兴趣——他们往往会违背自身经济利益投票。例如，纽约和旧金山的人们会支持加税的民主党，而堪萨斯州的人们则会投票给主张减税的共和党，结果他们收入更低，获得的政府福利也更少。我想开发一款工具，帮助人们了解总统政策提案对财务的影响。大四那年，我开发了一个网络应用程序，用户输入个人基本信息（如子女数量、年龄）后，系统就能计算出政策对税收和福利的具体影响，还能模拟不同政策对不同地区的影响。（00:07:40）这款应用迅速走红，尽管当时很少有人以这种视角看待政治，但在选举季我们吸引了400万用户。最初只是个获得资助的项目，最终却催生了Outline公司。多个政府部门联系我们，询问能否为其预算项目开发类似工具。马萨诸塞州州长甚至亲自飞来洽谈，成为我们的首位客户。我们成功拿下政府合同，加入Techstars加速器项目，并与奥巴马政府签约。然而开发过程中，政府停摆导致合同被取消。（00:08:51）我意识到自己并不擅长向政府销售软件，真正的核心能力是打造能在互联网上走红的产品。Outline并非政策模拟工具，我们向投资者坦白：“这不再是我们热衷的方向了。”提出退款并展示新创意，其中一款名为Five Labs的应用能通过分析Facebook帖子解析用户性格，其模型与剑桥分析公司使用的机制如出一辙，三天内吸引数千万用户。（00:10:09）借助该应用成功融资后，我们转向移动端，开发了地图、聊天、活动等各类应用，最终专注青少年市场。（00:10:55）青少年群体习惯易于塑造，随着年龄增长，用户会固化使用习惯，难以接受新事物。
我们发现成年人实际上并不常邀请他人加入新应用。研究发现，从13岁到18岁，用户邀请他人加入应用的数量几乎呈指数级下降。最重要的是，他们每天都会见面，这一点至关重要。消费者应用开发者有时会说吸烟者是锁定目标用户的绝佳群体，因为他们经常在建筑物外随意聚集。但这并不是说社交应用等同于香烟，我不太喜欢这种比喻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just on the note of you talking about why teens are important, I have this quote actually from you that I love where building on the point you made that for every social app I've ever built and the number of invitations sent per user drops 20% for every additional year of age from 13 to 18. If you build for adults, expect to acquire every user with ads, and I love that you have a very clear heuristic of per year, the amount of people they invite to the app is 20% lower.
turns.zh: 关于你谈到青少年为何重要的话题，我这里有一段引用你的话，我很喜欢。你提到过，每个我开发过的社交应用中，用户年龄每增加一岁（从13岁到18岁），用户发送邀请的数量就会下降20%。如果你针对成年人开发应用，就得靠广告获取每个用户。我很欣赏你用每年20%的降幅来清晰量化用户邀请量。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: If your users aren't inviting people to your app, you're going to have to find another way to acquire them, and that most likely means ads. If you're targeting older cohorts like adults, you're going to have to raise a huge amount of venture capital to finance that user acquisition pipeline and it's going to be extraordinarily expensive. As a seed stage up, it's going to be basically impossible to grow that user base, especially to get density if you need actual network effects among users.
turns.zh: 如果用户不主动邀请他人加入应用，你就得另辟蹊径获取用户，这很可能意味着要投放广告。如果你针对成年人等更成熟的用户群体，就得筹集巨额风险投资来支持用户获取渠道，但成本会极其高昂。作为初创阶段的公司，想要扩大用户基数基本是不可能的，尤其是在需要实现用户网络效应的情况下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Basically, you're building this help me decide who to vote for app that turned into a real business with government contracts coming to you trying to help you, pushing you to build something that you end up realizing I don't want to be doing this. Why am I building this app selling government contracts. What you did is you, and this is a really interesting lesson to take away, is you just realized, I don't want to be doing this. Investors don't force me to be working on this. I'm going to stop this. I'm going to go work on some other stuff that I'm actually excited about that I think has a bigger chance of success. That's where you transition to this startup studio where you're just trying a bunch of apps and I think it was called Midnight Labs, you said, something like that, right?
turns.zh: 基本上，你开发了一个帮助选举投票的应用，结果它变成了一个实实在在的商业项目，政府合同找上门来，但你逐渐意识到这不是你想做的。我为什么要开发这个卖政府合同的应用？你当时的觉悟非常宝贵，意识到“这不是我想做的。”投资者没有强迫你继续这个项目，你决定停手转向其他更令你兴奋、成功概率更高的项目。这就是你转型到创业工作室的转折点，你提到的那个叫Midnight Labs的团队，对吧？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Basically, I think that's a really interesting insight of just like if you're working on something you don't enjoy, you can change that, you can pivot, you can tell your investors I want to work on something else. Is there anything there that you want to add along those lines?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得这其实是个很有启发的洞见：如果你正在做不喜欢的项目，可以调整方向，告诉投资者你想转做其他事。这方面你还有什么补充吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: It was really hard for us to pivot to mobile. I think that was one of the most challenging things for me personally because it was a completely different paradigm. I actually have been building web apps since I was 12 years old. I built a full e-commerce business selling pirated games on the web, and I knew everything about growing a website. As we pivoted to mobile, I had to recalibrate my whole brain on how to do that. Mobile apps have such a low margin for error when it comes to designing them. Because I have this dogmatic view that every tap on a mobile app is a miracle for you as a product developer because users will turn and bounce to their next app very quickly. (00:14:46): If you actually sit behind someone and watch them use their phone, they actually switch between apps at a pretty high frequency. Every tap that you get, every single one is so scarce that you should be optimizing everything. I had to change my whole brain when we started pivoting to mobile and building these mobile apps, and it took a lot of failures. 14 of the apps that we launched were basically duds, and then we started fixating on teens and building apps for them. Eventually, we figured out an interesting heuristic for identifying consumer product opportunities that ultimately led us to tbh.
turns.zh: 向移动端转型对我们来说确实很困难。我认为这对我个人来说是最具挑战性的事情之一，因为这完全是一种不同的范式。我从12岁起就一直在开发网络应用程序。我曾在网上搭建过一个完整的盗版游戏销售电商平台，对网站增长的方方面面都了如指掌。但当我们转向移动端时，我不得不重新调整思维模式，彻底重构整个开发思路。移动应用在设计方面容不得半点差错，因为我秉持着一种教条——对产品开发者来说，用户在移动应用上的每一次点击都是奇迹，因为用户会很快切换到下一个应用并流失掉。（00:14:46）：如果你真的坐在别人身后观察他们使用手机，他们切换应用的频率其实非常高。每一次点击都极其宝贵，你必须对所有环节进行优化。向移动端转型并开发这些应用时，整个思维模式都需要彻底转变，我们经历了无数次失败。推出的14款应用几乎都是失败之作，后来我们开始专注于青少年群体，为他们开发应用。最终，我们找到了一个识别消费级产品机会的有趣启发，最终成就了tbh。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You spent four or five years trying a bunch of different ideas. I think people see this headline and we'll get into tbh of just like nine weeks after launch sells for $30 million to Facebook and everyone's like, "Oh, okay, that's amazing. I want that for my life." Nobody knows there's this four or five years of trying, you said 15 different apps before you got there, learning the things that actually work and don't work.
turns.zh: 你们花了四五年时间尝试各种不同的想法。我觉得人们看到这个标题时，会想到tbh在上线九周后就以3000万美元被Facebook收购，然后大家都感叹“哦，天哪，太棒了。我也想在生活中拥有这样的成功。”但没人知道这背后有四五年的尝试经历——你提到在成功之前尝试了15款不同的应用，不断总结哪些方法有效，哪些无效。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: We built 15 apps over the course of that pivot to consumer, and we built apps for every single app, map apps, chat apps, to-do lists. We just built every type of consumer app you could possibly think of. Also, we built for every audience too. We built for college students, we built for post-college. It was always very difficult to get the flywheel spinning for anyone after like 22 years old. That was the cutoff of when people just give up on adopting new products. It took us a few years to really internalize that, a lot of failures to realize no one needs another app after that age.
turns.zh: 在向消费级用户转型期间，我们开发了15款应用，涵盖地图应用、聊天应用、待办事项列表等各类消费级应用。我们几乎尝试了你能想到的所有消费级应用场景，同时针对不同用户群体进行优化。我们为大学生开发过应用，也为毕业后人群开发过应用。但22岁以上人群的增长势头始终难以启动，这正是人们放弃新产品尝试的临界点。我们花了几年时间才真正意识到这一点，也经历了无数次失败，才明白22岁以上用户对新应用的需求其实微乎其微。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The thing that you found there, which is really interesting because most people are building for people older than 22, that's a profound insight you had there. Every consumer app I see is trying to build for adults, and your lesson there is basically if you're trying to do that, you're probably going to need to raise money and spend a lot of money on paid ads.
turns.zh: 你在这里发现的洞察非常有趣，因为大多数人都在为22岁以上用户开发应用，而你的这番见解堪称深刻。市面上几乎所有消费级应用都致力于成人用户，但你的经验告诉我们，如果目标群体是22岁以上用户，必然需要大量融资并投放付费广告才能取得成功。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Most likely, you'll never get network effects. There's actually an interesting study many years ago that some academics in Spain did, I think it was in Spain, and they looked at how many people you text per year of your life, and it goes up very quickly from 14 to 18. It peaks around 21, so it's growing. The number of people you text is growing up until about 21, and then it just falls, it collapses, and then it comes back up at end of life. There's a few reasons all this happens, but basically, once you exit college, you reduce the number of contacts, your daily contacts. (00:17:48): Once you get married, it's even fewer. Then as you get older and your kids start having kids and you become a grandparent, you start texting again more or you join a retirement home. If you're building a product with network effects that's a communication tool, you want to be on that upward curve of adding connections to your social graph because then the urgency to connect is higher. If you really want to actually innovate at the edges of communication products, you really have to target that cohort that has the highest urgency to communicate, and that's teens.
turns.zh: 很可能你永远也无法获得网络效应。多年前西班牙的一些学者做过一项有趣的研究，他们研究了人们一生中每年发送短信的数量，结果显示从14岁到18岁，这一数字增长迅速，峰值出现在21岁左右，随后急剧下降，直到生命的最后阶段才再度回升。造成这种现象的原因有很多，但最根本的是，一旦你离开大学，日常社交圈的联系人数就会逐渐减少。（00:17:48）结婚后，联系人数量更是大幅缩减。随着年龄增长，当子女成家、自己成为祖父母后，人们会重新开始频繁发短信，或者选择入住养老院。如果你要开发一款具有网络效应的通信工具产品，就需要抓住社交图谱中新增联系人的上升曲线，因为这时候人们的社交需求最为迫切。若想在通信产品领域真正创新，就必须锁定那些沟通需求最为迫切的群体——青少年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you found these things out, not through just research and not through just thinking, it was through actual trying things over and over and over and trying different audiences, trying different experiences. A lot of people see your advice and they're like, "How does he know?" It's just you've done all these things yourself. You've seen them, you're sitting there watching teens use these apps. I think very few people actually do that, and they just come up with these theories that aren't based in empirical evidence.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你能通过反复尝试和观察不同用户群体、不同使用场景来发现这些规律。很多人看到你的建议会问：“他怎么会知道这些？”因为你亲身实践过。你亲眼见证过青少年使用这些应用的全过程。我认为很少有人能做到这一点，他们往往只是凭空提出一些没有实证依据的理论。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: We got pretty good at building these apps. I think our first mobile app took us about a year, and then our last one took us about two weeks. We also got very good at testing apps. The most important thing that I often instruct teams to do is to develop a reproducible testing process, and that will actually influence the probability of your success more than anything. It's so unpredictable whether a consumer product idea will work. If you actually focus more on your process for taking many shots at bat, that's what actually reduces the risk more than anything. We figured out ways to seed apps into schools. We also, during the course of that company, we figured out how to seed it into affinity groups, hobbyists, things like that. We were on app number 15, a lot of failures during the course of this company, and I remember a lot of our team members were like, "I kind of want to leave. I think this is it for me." (00:20:08): One of our key team members actually put in their two weeks' notice. The day before we launched our final app, we were getting kind of low on money. I was tired. I called our lawyer to ask, how do you dissolve a company? I messaged a few mentors saying like, one people that have been through it, and I said, "What are the steps to do this?" Then I had a conversation on the way out with that team member that wanted to leave, and I said, "I understand, but what if the app actually starts charting on the App Store?" He said, "What are the chances of that? You know that's not going to happen." I said, "Sure, okay." We launched this app and it was a polling app, tbh, and it immediately took off in the school that we seeded it into, in Georgia. We picked the one school that had the earliest start date in the United States because we needed to launch as soon as possible, given the state of the company. (00:21:26): I think it spread to 40% of the school downloaded it in the first 24 hours and it rapidly spread to the neighboring schools. Suddenly, I was like, "Oh, we might have something here." Servers started crashing and watching it climb the charts. I looked at our numbers and I'm like, "We will be number one in the United States in six days." Then I looked at our Amazon bill and it was like 120,000. I looked at our bank account, it said 150,000. I'm like, "Okay, these two numbers don't really..." I quickly had to put together a funding round and I told my team, "Can you guys just pause for two months and just really focus on this? I think I could probably sell this thing." It turned into a pretty competitive bidding process, actually. There was a really, really great moment where there was one of the acquirers, or one of the bidders was based in LA, had told me to fly down, and they told me to fly down that day. (00:22:40): I got on a plane, went to the airport without a ticket, showed up. When we were rolling out this app, we were doing a state-by-state rollout strategy where every state was geo-fenced. We hadn't launched California until that morning. I arrived at this company, this founders in LA's house, and he said, "Show me the metrics. You guys are like, what? Number four or something?" Since we just launched California, it's a big state. I said, "No, we're actually number one. We're the number one app in the United States." He said, "Show me the metrics." Our CTO, Erik Hazzard, is a published author in mapping. He created an amazing dashboard that could show real-time installs on a map. It was around 4:00 PM and school had just gotten out, so I zoomed in on the block that we were having that meeting, and the entire block was lit up with installs all around us. Then that's what got the ball rolling on a... It was a really, really like, cinematic moment of showing something that you created that literally just took over the entire neighborhood around you.
turns.zh:
我们的应用开发能力已经相当不错了。我记得我们的第一个移动应用花了大约一年的时间开发，最后一个应用只用了两周。我们在应用测试方面也做得很出色。我常告诫团队要建立可重复的测试流程，这比任何其他因素都更能影响成功概率。判断一个消费级产品是否能成功实在太难预测了。如果你更专注于如何多次尝试开发新应用，实际上这比任何其他措施都更能降低风险。

 我们找到了在学校推广应用的办法。在公司运营期间，我们还成功地将应用植入了兴趣小组、爱好者社区等圈子。在开发第15款应用时，公司经历了多次失败。记得当时很多团队成员都说：“我有点想离开了，这次可能就是我的终点了。”（00:20:08） 有一位核心成员提前两周提交了离职通知。就在我们即将发布最后一款应用的前一天，我们的资金链快要断裂了。我疲惫不堪地打电话问律师如何解散公司，还联系了曾经历过类似情况的导师，询问具体步骤。最后在离开公司前，我和那位想离职的团队成员聊了聊：“我理解你的感受，但如果这款应用在App Store上火了呢？” 他说：“这种可能性有多大？你知道这根本不可能。” 我说：“好吧，那就试试看。” 我们推出的这款投票应用在乔治亚州的试点学校迅速走红，首日下载量就占到该校学生总数的40%，并迅速扩展到周边学校。突然间，我意识到：“哦，或许我们真能做成点事！” 服务器崩溃，应用排名一路攀升。我查看数据时发现：六天内我们就能登上全美应用排行榜榜首。随后亚马逊账单显示欠费12万美元，银行账户余额15万美元。我暗想：“这两个数字怎么对不上啊……” 我紧急筹备融资轮次，对团队说：“暂停两个月，专注于此事。我觉得这款产品应该能卖出去。” 结果竞标异常激烈。其中一位收购方或竞标者位于洛杉矶，当天就约我飞过去见面。

 (00:22:40) 我登上飞机，没有票就冲进机场，赶到洛杉矶创始人家里。他说：“给我看数据，你们说什么？第四名？” 由于刚上线加州市场，这里可是个大州。我说：“不，我们是第一名，美国第一的应用。” 他要求查看实时数据。我们的CTO埃里克·哈扎德是地图领域的知名学者，他开发了一个能实时显示安装数据的地图仪表盘。下午四点刚放学，我把视角拉近到会议所在街区，数据显示下载量激增。
整个街区被灯光装置照亮，四周到处都是装置艺术品。正是这一幕拉开了序幕……那真是一个极具电影感的瞬间，你展示的作品简直占据了整个社区的视野。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's insane. That's going to be in the movie of Nikita Bier in the future. A couple of questions here. One, you predicted the chart, you would hit number one. What does it take to hit number one? What is the number you're looking at? Is it some number downloads to get to number one in the App Store?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。这会在尼基塔·比尔（Nikita Bier）的电影里出现的。这里有几个问题。首先，你预测图表会登上榜首。要登上榜首需要什么？你关注的具体数字是多少？在App Store上登上榜首需要多少下载量？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: It fluctuates. It used to be like 80 to 100,000 installs, but now you have these companies that are just spending extraordinary amounts on ads and or injecting it into one of their other apps. Between Threads, Temu and all these other apps that are spending on acquisition and all that, some days it's up to 300,000.
turns.zh: 这个数字波动很大。以前大概是8万到10万次安装，但现在有些公司在广告上投入巨资，或者把用户引流到其他应用。Threads、Temu等应用在获客方面投入巨大，有时候一天就能达到30万次安装。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's per day?
turns.zh: 这是每天的数据吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. Amazing.
turns.zh: 天哪，太惊人了。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: At the peak of tbh, we were getting 360,000 per day.
turns.zh: 在tbh达到峰值时，我们每天有36万次安装。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other two things I want to spend a little time on here before we move on to the next app is, what was the insight that helped you come up with this is a big idea that we should try? Then what was the insight into how to spread this so virally? I know that one is really close.
turns.zh: 接下来转到下一个应用之前，我想再花点时间探讨两个问题：是什么样的洞察帮助你想出这个值得尝试的创意？然后又是如何让它如此迅速地传播开来的？我知道其中一个答案很接近了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... to how to spread this so virally, and I know that one is really clever.
turns.zh: ……关于如何让它如此迅速传播的，我知道其中一个答案非常巧妙。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: After building all these apps, we had these kind of lingering users that stuck around and would share feedback with us on our next app. And so there were a couple, like there's a senior in high school that I would send screenshots of our products. He told me about this trend called TBH that kids were playing on Snapchat, where they would post an image of a bunch of emojis and it would say like, "I like you. Your smart. Your style is great." And you would just reply to the story with the emoji of what you felt. And I was like, "This is kind of weird. You post this on your story and then people send you feedback." And I'm like, "So teens are looking for this vehicle for disclosure essentially." And I'm like, "That's kind of cool. I wonder if you could make that into an app." We had sketched some things out. As we were sketching things out, I looked on the app store, and the number one app in the United States was an app called Sarahah. It was for sending anonymous messages by adding a link to your Snapchat story. (00:26:17): But the thing that was most interesting was the entire app was in Arabic. The number one app in the United States was in Arabic. And that was one of the most strongest signal that you could ever have that people want something. And so when I meet with founders, I often tell them like, "The way you should be searching for product ideas is this concept of latent demand where people are trying to obtain a particular value and going through a very distortive process to obtain that value." And if you can actually crystallize what their motivation is and build a product around and clear up what they're trying to actually do, you can have this kind of intense adoption. (00:27:11): When we saw what people were doing with Sarahah, I also looked at some of the tweets and comments on it. A lot of people were receiving negative messages. And so what I saw with the game that kids were playing on Snapchat TBH and then Sarahah, I realized just people want to know good things about themselves and that they don't want these bullying messages that they're getting on these anonymous apps, and I was like, "Well, what if instead of actually typing what you wanted to say about somebody, you just answered polls and we authored those polls so that we ensured everything would always be positive?" (00:27:51): I mean, in the back of my head, I always knew anonymous apps go viral, but they always lead to these awful news stories of kids committing suicide, self-harm and all that. And so I was like, "I'll never build anything like that." But when we came up with this new mechanic where you could only say positive things through polls, who has the best smile, who's most likely to be president, and then you receive it as anonymous, but your name is selected, what we discovered a couple of things is it made users feel a lot better. It actually solved what they were trying to do and they also sent a much higher volume of messages. And so it was literally explosive adoption. (00:28:35): One school I was looking at, they sent 450,000 messages in the first seven days of adopting it. And when you look at day one volume of messages sent on a messaging app, you're lucky if people send three or four or something, but we were sending 60 and we couldn't even handle it, so we had to geofence the app because we needed to scale our servers, which is actually a pretty controversial decision inside of our company, because why would you turn off something that's working? But at my core, I knew if it's working at this many individual schools, we could just relaunch it any time and it'll go viral. So let's regroup and figure out what's happening here and then relaunch.
turns.zh:
开发了这么多应用后，我们发现有一些忠实用户会留下来，并会给我们下一款应用提供反馈。其中有个高中生，我会给他发产品截图。他跟我提到了Snapchat上流行的TBH趋势——用户会发布一堆表情符号的图片，配文类似“我喜欢你，你很聪明，你的风格很棒”。用户回复时只需选择对应表情即可。我当时觉得这挺奇怪的，用户把这些信息发布到动态里，然后别人再回复。于是我联想到，青少年们其实是在寻找一种公开表达情感的渠道。这想法挺酷的，我好奇能否把它做成应用。我们做了些初步设计时，发现美国应用商店排名第一的Sarahah应用竟是阿拉伯语界面。这个现象强有力地表明，人们对某种产品的需求是存在的。所以我常跟创业者说，寻找产品灵感的关键在于挖掘用户潜在需求——当人们试图获取某种价值，却因种种阻碍而难以实现时，就需要一个产品来化解这些阻碍。若能准确理解用户动机，并围绕这些动机打造产品，就能获得爆炸式增长。

观察Sarahah的用户行为后，我发现很多人收到负面评价。这让我联想到Snapchat上的匿名互动游戏TBH，以及Sarahah的核心玩法——用户通过匿名投票表达积极评价。比如“谁笑得最美？”“谁最有可能当总统？”这些互动机制不仅提升了用户体验，还有效规避了匿名平台带来的负面影响。用户反馈热情高涨，短短七天内就发送了45万条消息。这在即时通讯应用中实属罕见，我们甚至因服务器负载不得不限制地理范围——这在公司内部引发了激烈讨论，毕竟谁会主动关闭成功的产品？但我坚信，只要单个学校能成功应用，我们就能推广到更广阔的市场。
随时重新发布它，它就会迅速传播开来。所以，让我们重新整合思路，搞清楚现在的情况，然后再重新发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you keep talking about how went viral and crazy, grew like crazy. I know that there's a little trick that you came up with to help it spread. Can you just briefly talk about what you did there and to help it spread so quickly within a school?
turns.zh: 好吧，你一直在说这个应用如何迅速走红、疯狂增长。我知道你想出了个小技巧来助推传播，能不能简单讲讲你们是怎么做到的，以及它为何能在学校里迅速传播开来？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I think you're referring to, there's a memo that was leaked to BuzzFeed while I was at Facebook. The main thing we found was like, to be convinced to download an app, you need to see it. You need to see the marketing message three times or so. So you basically need to saturate an area with every kind of marketing you can. So we ran ads targeted at a particular school to when we were seeding and testing these apps. And we also followed people creating a dedicated Instagram account that went to that school, because we learned that high schoolers identify their school in their bio, so it says RHS on their bio. And so that was how we tried to get the entire school to adopt synchronously. We'd follow them and then accept the followbacks. (00:30:36): Big misunderstanding though, and I get this DM a lot of people are like, "I'm trying to replicate your strategy. We've just done it at 15 schools and it's not working anymore." This is not the way we grew the app. This is how we tested apps. Really, it's a little bit nuanced there. That's an important nuance because you need to get enough intensity of adoption and density for a social network to start to get the flywheel spinning, but the app should grow by itself after that. And people think we just went from school to school following every kid on it. You can't, that's totally unrealistic. But for the first 100 users, yes, that's how we got them. And that allowed us to know whether the product was working or not. We could get enough people on it and then we could, with conviction, say that whether the app had legs and we wouldn't have this kind of uncertainty like, "Oh, did they add enough friends? Did we get enough people on it? Did they reach the aha moment because you need friends to get on?" (00:31:41): So we wanted to eliminate that confounding variable, and so we figured out a way to just get a bunch of people to adopt at once. And that's one thing I encourage a lot of founders to do, is figure out a way to eliminate all those potentially confounding variables so you can know immediately whether something's working or not. You never want to walk away from an experiment or test and say, "Well, maybe the execution was bad because it takes a lot of energy to mobilize a team to test something," and you really want to make sure your tests actually provide signal.
turns.zh: 我觉得你说的是我在Facebook工作时，某份备忘录被泄露给了BuzzFeed。我们发现，要让用户下载应用，关键在于让他们看到广告。用户需要看到营销信息至少三次。所以你需要用各种营销手段覆盖目标区域。我们在测试应用时，会针对特定学校投放定向广告，还会关注创建专属Instagram账号的用户，这些账号通常会标注所在学校，比如RHS（Rock Hill High School）。这样就能让整个学校同步采用应用。我们会关注这些用户并接受他们的互粉请求。（00:30:36）：但很多人误解了。他们发私信问：“我想复制你们的策略，我们在15所学校试过，但现在不行了。”这不是我们推广应用的正确方法。这只是测试应用的手段。关键在于让应用获得足够的用户基础，让社交网络的飞轮开始运转，但之后应用应该能自然增长。人们以为我们挨个学校去加用户，但这根本不现实。前100个用户确实是这样获取的，但关键在于通过这个数据判断产品是否可行。（00:31:41）：所以我们要消除这些干扰因素，想办法一次性让大量用户采用。我建议创业者也这么做，找到消除干扰因素的方法，这样就能立即判断产品是否成功。千万别在实验结束后说：“可能执行不到位”，因为动员团队测试很费精力，而你真正需要的是能提供有效信号的数据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So your advice here is when you're testing something, test the best possible version of what that could be, whether it takes manual work or something that is never going to scale, test the ideal. Because that'll tell you, " Even if this could be the best possible version, do people actually care?"
turns.zh: 所以你的建议是测试时，要尽可能测试最理想的版本，哪怕手动操作、短期无法规模化，也要测试最优解。这能让你知道：“即使这是最优版本，用户真的会买账吗？”

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah, we would try to get an entire school to adopt, just to know if everyone had 10 friends, would they actually derive value from this app? We also did other things, and I recommend all companies do this, is put live chat customer support in your app 24 hours a day. It sounds insane. It's like the whole point of tech is you don't need to do that. That's the whole point of a software. But then users get this white glove experience, and that eliminates another confounding variable, like did they think their problems were solved or they were treated well? But most of all, one of the reasons I actually recommend people put live chat in their app is it's the best vehicle for getting feedback and doing user research because users will literally tell you the problem they're having. So we had our person that was running this. He's name is Michael Gutierrez. He's done it for all my companies actually. He's the community and customer support rep. He would paste any interesting feedback into Slack and then we would be like, "Oh, this user has a great idea. We should consider turning that into a feature." So you really want your finger on the pulse as you roll these things out so you can get a sense for what's working, what isn't, and also make users feel great and make sure at the end they promote your app positively to their peers.
turns.zh: 是的，我们曾尝试让整个学校都采用这款应用，只是想看看如果每个人都有10个朋友，他们是否真的能从这款应用中获得价值。我们还做了其他尝试，我建议所有公司都应该这样做——在应用中24小时提供实时聊天客服支持。这听起来很疯狂。科技的意义不就在于无需这样做吗？这才是软件的本质。但用户能获得这种贴心服务，就能消除另一个混杂变量，比如他们是否认为自己的问题被解决了，或者得到了良好的对待？但最重要的是，我之所以建议在应用中加入实时聊天功能，是因为这是获取反馈和进行用户研究的最佳途径，因为用户会直接告诉你他们遇到的问题。所以我们让负责这项工作的人——迈克尔·古铁雷斯（Michael Gutierrez）——来做这件事。他实际上为我所有的公司都做过这项工作。他是社区和客户支持代表。他会把任何有趣的反馈粘贴到Slack上，然后我们会说：“哦，这个用户有个很棒的主意。我们应该考虑把它做成一个功能。”所以在推出这些功能时，你真的需要时刻掌握用户动态，这样才能了解哪些有效，哪些无效，同时让用户感觉良好，并确保他们最终会积极向同龄人推荐你的应用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that piece of advice. (00:34:11): Okay, so to close out the TBH chapter, is there anything else that you think is important for people to know or any other lasting lessons from that part of your journey that you bring with you to new apps that you're building today?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个建议。（00:34:11）：好的，关于TBH这部分，最后还有什么你认为对人们来说很重要，或者从你这段旅程中获得的持久教训，可以带入你今天正在开发的新应用中吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I think the thing that is hard to really understand for first-time founders that hit breakout success with a consumer product is how draining and how spread thin you get, because everything breaks. Everything that you built needs to be substituted almost every three days. (00:34:52): I can just give you an example. We were just talking about this customer support system that we had. The first system broke after three days. The next one broke seven days later, we had to replace it with a different one that could scale even better. And if you think about that on every dimension of the company, it is absolute chaos to keep the thing online as it scales up. And so you have to be ruthless with prioritization as something scales up and put out the largest fires first, because that was something that I didn't really fully understand, is how many things go wrong. And if we didn't geofence the app, there would be no way we would've been able to keep that thing online because that gave us some slack to control growth.
turns.zh: 我认为对于首次创办成功消费级产品的创始人来说，真正难以理解的是，当一切都出问题时，你会变得多么疲惫不堪，分身乏术，因为每件事都会出故障。你构建的每样东西几乎每三天就需要更换一次。（00:34:52）：我可以给你举个例子。我们刚刚谈到我们的客户支持系统。第一个系统用了三天就崩溃了。下一个系统七天后又崩溃了，我们不得不换成一个能更好扩展的系统。如果你从公司的每个维度去考虑，随着规模扩大保持系统在线简直就是一场混乱。所以当事情扩展时，你必须无情地进行优先级排序，先解决最紧急的问题，因为这才是我真正不完全理解的地方——出问题的频率太高了。如果我们没有对应用进行地理围栏，根本不可能保持它在线，因为这样能给我们一些控制增长的缓冲时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good example of when people ask like, "Hey, does my app have product-market fit?" I think this is an example of this is what it looks like when things are breaking every three days when you have to geofence it to keep it from crashing.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的例子，当人们问“嘿，我的应用有产品-市场契合度吗？”时，我认为这就是当每三天就出问题时，你需要对应用进行地理围栏以防止崩溃的真实写照。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: A lot of people ask me like, "What's the benchmark for product-market fit?" And this founder that I'm friends with, his name's Roger Dickey, he told me this one time, "If your product's working, you'll know. And if there's any uncertainty, it's not working." And it really is a binary when it comes to consumer products. People are going to be fighting to get into it and you'll find new measures that you've never heard of like, "Our metric was hourly actives per day." Not daily active users, hourly active users. So you'll start seeing that and it'll be abundantly obvious what product-market fit is. You'll know it when you see it is the bottom line.
turns.zh: 很多人问我：“产品与市场契合度的标准是什么？” 我认识的一位创业者罗杰·迪基曾对我说：“如果产品真的成功，你自然能感知到。若存在任何不确定性，那说明它就不成功。” 对于消费类产品而言，这确实是个非黑即白的判断标准。用户会争相涌入，你会发现一些前所未闻的衡量指标，比如“每日用户小时活跃量”（而非“每日活跃用户数”）。当你看到这些数据时，产品与市场契合度的含义就一目了然——只要你亲眼见证了它，就能心领神会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you launch TBH, it goes viral, start getting offers from companies. Nine weeks later after launch, you end up selling it to Facebook. What was it like selling your company and then what was it like working at Facebook? Which you worked at for four years. I was not expecting that when I was looking at your LinkedIn. So yeah, what was it like selling? What was it like working at Facebook?
turns.zh: 好的，你推出了TBH，产品迅速走红，开始收到各大公司的收购邀约。推出九周后，你最终将其卖给了Facebook。能把公司卖掉是怎样一种体验？在Facebook工作的四年又如何？我看你的领英资料时，完全没想到你有过这样的经历。那么，出售公司的过程是怎样的？在Facebook工作又有怎样的感受？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Selling your company is one of the most draining processes you could ever go through as a founder. When we met with Facebook, they told me they have 80 people assigned to this deal. And I'm like, I have one person, it's just me. They were like the SWAT team of M&A. (00:37:45): The funniest part was they wanted to meet the team as well. And so they came out to our office in Oakland, which is a dingy old office that I got for $1,800 a month. That was our rent for the office. They arrive and they walk in. There's two engineers and one designer and me, and they're just like, "This is the whole company? This is the number one app in the United States?" I'm like, "Yeah, this is it." And when we went there, when we arrived, we joined the youth team, which was about, I don't know, 150 people just for this one division of Facebook. It was my first job effectively that I've ever had. (00:38:31): When they told me my title, they said I would be a product manager, I was like, "Okay, I don't know exactly what that is, but yeah, I guess that's what I do." I arrive and then I get access to a workplace system where people post all the things they're working on, and I realized it's kind of like this almost academic environment for social networks, like social network development. It's like the Harvard of social networks. I was reading all these studies that people were doing on like, "Oh, if we change that, this is the impact to retention and DAU." I was so impressed, like, "There's a whole science here." (00:39:20): A lot of the stuff that we did was learned from first principles, but then we saw it actually turn into systems and processes here. But the thing I didn't realize as a product manager in a large tech company is there is very little product management that you do. You're actually not as involved in the product as I had assumed. I thought, "Oh, you're the person who gets in the pixels and designs the flows." Absolutely not. You're completely detached from the design process. There's a design vertical org that does all that and they don't really want you working on that. So that was very difficult for me because when people ask me like, "What do you think you're good at?" At the core, I'm a designer. I don't consider myself a product manager. I'm great at growing things, looking at mixed panel and then designing the things that make it grow. But there's a rift between those two things inside of a large tech company. (00:40:27): And so I loved the academic approach to growing, but it was really hard for me personally as I became disconnected from the design process. I think that a lot of my skills atrophied over those four years. But I did stick around. I went through multiple orgs. Favorite one at the end was new product experimentation where I worked with other founders, a bunch of legends in Silicon Valley, building zero to one products, standalone apps. I mean, I was building standalone apps my entire time at Facebook. I think I built probably eight apps while I was at Facebook.
turns.zh:
出售公司是创业者所经历的最令人精疲力竭的过程之一。当我们与Facebook会面时，他们告诉我，他们有80个人专门负责这笔交易。我当时就想，我只有一个人，就我一个人。他们简直是并购领域的特警队。（00:37:45）：最有趣的是，他们还想见见我们的团队。于是他们来到我们位于奥克兰的办公室，那是一个破旧的老办公室，我每月花1800美元租下来。这就是我们办公室的租金。他们一到办公室，就走了进来。办公室里有两个工程师、一个设计师和我，他们惊讶地问：“这就是整个公司？这就是美国排名第一的应用？”我回答：“是的，就是这样。”我们到那里后，加入了一个青年团队，大约有150人，就为了Facebook的这个部门。这是我真正意义上第一份工作。
（00:38:31）：当他们告诉我我的职位时，说我将担任产品经理，我当时想：“好吧，我不知道这具体是什么意思，但我想，这就是我的工作吧。”我到了那里，然后获得了访问工作系统的机会，人们在那里发布他们正在做的事情，我意识到这几乎就像一个社交网络开发的学术环境。这里是社交网络的哈佛大学。我阅读了人们正在进行的各种研究，比如“如果我们改变这个，对留存率和DAU有什么影响”。我印象深刻，心想：“这里有整个一套科学体系。”
（00:39:20）：我们所做的大部分工作都是从第一性原理出发学习的，但在这里我们看到它实际上变成了系统和流程。但作为一家大型科技公司的产品经理，我没有意识到自己要做的产品管理工作非常少。实际上，产品管理工作比我想象的要少得多。我原以为，“哦，你就是那个负责像素级设计、设计流程的人。”完全不是这样。你与设计过程完全脱节。有一个专门的设计部门来做这些，他们并不希望你参与其中。所以这对我来说很困难。当人们问我：“你认为自己擅长什么？”我核心上是一个设计师。我不认为自己是产品经理。我擅长推动增长，研究混合面板，然后设计能促进增长的东西。但在大型科技公司里，这两者之间存在着鸿沟。
（00:40:27）：所以我喜欢这种学术式的增长方法，但对我个人来说真的很难，因为我与设计过程脱节了。我认为这四年里我的很多技能都荒废了。但我还是坚持了下来。我换了多个部门。最后最喜欢的部门是新产品实验室，在那里我与其他创始人合作，遇到了硅谷的许多传奇人物，开发从零到一的产品，独立应用。我在Facebook的整个时间里都在开发独立应用。我想我在Facebook期间大概开发了八个应用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: But it is much, much more difficult to build apps at a large company. A lot of the insights that you have are not things that you can necessarily present or put in writing in a VP meeting, like, " We're building an app for teens to flirt." That probably is not what you would present to a bunch of McKinsey consultants at. So I think that makes it really difficult to be completely intellectually honest about what you're building. And when the team isn't honest about it, then it's really hard to iterate toward the right thing in that context. Having said that, there's a lot of things you don't have to deal with as a product... I don't have to deal think about money, I don't have to think about paying legal bills or doing finance and accounting. So all that's abstracted away, but there is regulatory stuff that you have to deal with that I had zero exposure to as a founder of a small company.
turns.zh: 然而，在大公司开发应用程序要困难得多得多。你所拥有的许多洞察力，并非是可以在VP会议上口头或书面呈现的，比如“我们正在为青少年开发一款约会应用”。这种想法很可能不会在麦肯锡顾问面前被提及。因此，在这种情况下，要完全诚实地表达你正在开发的产品的真实意图，实在是件难事。当团队成员不坦诚时，要朝着正确的方向迭代就更是难上加难。话虽如此，作为产品经理，你无需处理许多事务……我无需操心资金问题，也无需处理法律账单或财务会计事务。所有这些都被抽象化了，但确实有监管方面的要求，这些是我作为小公司创始人从未接触过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: An insight you're sharing there potentially is the reason a company like Facebook isn't amazing at launching completely new product, zero to one stuff, is they might be a little too risk averse and it's hard to talk about stuff that people actually really, really want deeply. Is that kind of the sense there?
turns.zh: 你提到的见解或许能解释为什么像Facebook这样的公司在推出全新产品（从零到一的创新）方面表现不佳——因为他们可能过于规避风险，难以谈论人们真正渴望的东西。是这样理解的吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: It's hard to really verbalize some of the things that motivate us as people. There's a tweet I put out that's kind of dogmatic in terms of how I view why people download apps and it's very simple. It's like people download apps to make or save money. Examples of that might be like WhatsApp, where free texting. And then the other reason is to find a mate, so maybe like Tinder or Snapchat, find love. And the third is to unplug from reality maybe like Netflix or Fortnite. There's a bunch of other kind of subcategories that are very utilitarian like movement, Uber or Airbnb, like shelter. And so I think putting that in a framing document and the particular nuanced reason why people are going to adopt is difficult when you're presenting that to people that are seasoned professionals and care about how something might reflect on them personally. (00:43:51): And so that's really difficult inside of a large company. You'd certainly have distribution advantages. If you want to just inject your app into one of the parent apps and get density within a community, you could do that. But that part I think is probably solvable for a startup if you just want to pay for ads. Getting your app into a dense friend graph is overall trivial. As a founder, you should be able to pull it off after enough tries. So that advantage that a big company brings, I mean it makes it easier, but it's not something that I think is something that a founder can't solve for themselves.
turns.zh: 要真正表达一些激励我们的内在因素实在不易。我曾发过一条推文，比较狗血地总结了人们下载应用的动机：要么赚钱，要么省钱。比如WhatsApp免费发短信；Tinder、Snapchat之类的约会应用；Netflix、Fortnite之类的娱乐消遣；Uber、Airbnb之类的实用工具……但要把这些洞察转化为框架文件，准确传达人们为何会采用某款应用，却很难，尤其是面对经验丰富的专业人士时，他们更关注产品对自身形象的反馈。（00:43:51）这在大公司内部确实是个难题。当然，分发优势是存在的。如果你想将应用嵌入母公司应用，借助其庞大用户群体推广，确实可行。但对于初创公司而言，投放广告就能解决问题。让应用融入密集的社交圈，本质上并不复杂。作为创始人，只要尝试足够次数，应该就能做到。因此，大公司的优势固然能带来便利，但我认为初创者自己也能克服这些挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So an interesting takeaway it sounds like is many people feel like, "I'm going to build a social app." They probably often hear, "Facebook's going to do that. Instagram's going to copy you. Snap's going to do that." And what I'm hearing here is it's not as easy as many people think, that it might be actually a lot harder for them to try something.
turns.zh: 所以听起来一个有趣的启示是，许多人会说：“我要开发一款社交应用。” 他们可能常听到：“Facebook要做这个。Instagram要抄袭你了。Snap也要做这个了。” 而我在这里听到的是，这远比很多人想象的要难得多，他们要尝试新事物可能面临诸多挑战。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: It's not only harder for them to identify these opportunities and to verbalize it internally and align the company around it. It's also hard to respond to signals in the market. A lot of people think these incumbents are going to steal your ideas. And for the most part, it takes a pretty long time for them to respond to even the number one app or charting in the app because it'll start charting in the app store, a PM will make a post about it. And then the market's strategy or market research team might do a study to follow up on it. It'll kind of float around for a few months. They might put together a framing deck saying, "Hey, we should go after this opportunity. Let's put together this team. It'll go through VP reviews. And then it'll start development. Development might take six to 12 months." Realistically, I think most companies, large companies take 12 to 24 months to respond to competitive threats in the market.
turns.zh: 他们不仅更难识别这些机遇、在内部清晰表达并动员全公司围绕机遇行动，还难以对市场信号作出快速响应。许多人认为，这些行业巨头会窃取你的创意。但实际上，即便面对市场头部应用或图表趋势，巨头们的反应也极为迟缓——应用商店数据出现后，产品经理可能发布一篇分析报告，随后市场策略或研究团队才会启动跟进研究。整个过程通常要耗时数月：他们可能会整理一份框架文档，提出“我们应该抓住这个机遇，组建团队”；随后经过副总裁层级审批；再启动开发阶段，周期可能长达6至12个月。现实来看，大多数大公司需要12至24个月才能应对市场竞争威胁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think this is solvable? Is there something a company can change to get better at this? Are there companies that are good at this in your experience, or is this just as you grow, this is just what happens?
turns.zh: 你认为这个问题能解决吗？企业可以通过哪些改变来提升应对能力？以你的经验来看，有哪些公司在这方面做得好？还是说这只是随着企业发展自然形成的现象？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: The incentives within large companies make this very difficult, because you don't want to present something that you have a hunch about being a good idea because if there's not market signals already, then it's hard to defend. People in companies are focused on getting their yearly bonus or they're focused on their performance reviews. It's hard to show up into a framing meeting saying like... And a framing meeting is a meeting where you are positioning the opportunity and everything, "Here's what we should go after." It's hard to just say, "Okay, by first principles, this is a good idea and here's some very vague market signals." In reality, you need to walk in and say, "Here's the number one app in the United States and we don't own it." If you present something like that, that's pretty defensible if you fail because there was market evidence. But if you fail about something that's more based on kind of vague abstract... (00:47:19): So you have to, generally, the only path is to copy existing products if you want to really get momentum inside of a large organization. And for completely new concepts, it's I think very difficult to present a lot of those ideas, either to verbalize them into a document or to even get rally the organization around it.
turns.zh: 大企业的内部激励机制让这一切变得异常困难，因为人们不愿贸然提出仅凭直觉认为可行的想法。若市场信号尚未显现，防御性辩护就会面临挑战。企业员工往往专注于年度奖金或绩效评估，很难在框架会议上放声主张——这类会议本应是定位机遇、整合资源的场所。若你只说"基于第一性原理，这是一个好点子，但市场信号尚不明确"，根本站不住脚。相反，你必须直接陈述："这是美国头号应用，我们却未能将其收入囊中"。若能提供此类有力证据，即便失败也易于辩解。但若基于模糊抽象概念提案，成功概率微乎其微。(00:47:19)：因此，在大企业内部，想要真正推动创新，通常只能复制现有产品。至于全新的概念，要么难以转化为文档，要么难以凝聚全公司共识。
