turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: The functional organization structure of big tech has kind of separated product managers from the product development process in many ways. They're not looking at data because data scientists are doing that. They're just parsing some of the reports that they get back. They're mainly just writing documents and then kind of being the team secretary and running around, getting approvals from each cross-functional team, legal privacy, everything like that. And yeah, you're actually very much separated from the product itself. And so I think what Snapchat has done, and I think Apple too, to the same extent, is that designers run the show. And I think that's led to some very novel-
turns.zh: 大型科技公司的职能型组织架构在诸多方面将产品经理与产品开发流程割裂开来。他们无需关注数据，因为数据科学家会处理这些工作。他们只是解析收到的部分报告。他们主要负责撰写文档，充当团队秘书，在各个跨职能团队间奔波协调，获取法律隐私方面的批准等等。实际上，你与产品本身严重脱节。因此，我认为Snapchat（以及苹果在某种程度上）所采取的做法是让设计师主导全局。我认为这催生了一些极具创新性的成果——

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: And I think that's led to some very novel products coming out from both of those companies. But I mean that is its own host of problems because actually rolling out a product inside of a large organization, it requires a sheer force of will because it's a lot of work. I mean, there's a lot of regulatory scrutiny, scaling it up. You do need someone to project manage. And so I don't know if it's the silver bullet as to give designers the reign to run the show, but I also don't think the current traditional like Google, Facebook style of being team secretaries is also the best solution.
turns.zh: 并且我认为这促使这两家公司推出了许多极具创新性的产品。但这也带来了一系列问题，因为在大型组织内部推出新产品需要强大的意志力——毕竟这项工作繁琐重重。监管审查、规模化扩张等环节都需要专人统筹管理。我不确定让设计师全权主导产品开发是否万能良方，但我也认为谷歌、Facebook等公司那种团队秘书式的传统管理模式未必是最佳解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To defend product managers, I think many product managers spend a lot of time in design, spend a lot of time with data science. I think probably what you saw is like the extreme big, big, big tech version of product management. I know even PMs at Facebook can if they want to spend time with design. I think it's just obviously very different from a startup world where you're just, that's all you're doing.
turns.zh: 为产品经理辩护一下，我认为许多产品经理确实会投入大量时间在设计和数据科学方面。我觉得你所见到的可能只是大型科技公司产品管理的极端放大版。我知道即便在Facebook，产品经理如果愿意，也可以投入大量精力在设计上。这显然与初创公司的情形大不相同——在初创公司，产品经理就是专注于这些核心工作。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah, it's certainly an exaggerated view, but it's particularly relevant I think for all the zero to one initiatives because if you're a product manager on a standalone app inside of a large, like you should be designing the hierarchy, the pixels, the flows, everything. And then yeah, it should be cleaned up prototype by a technical designer, but that's your idea. And products live and die in the pixels, like consumer products, so that's on you. And that's where I think for maybe larger growth initiatives, yes, you can be a little more detached from the pixels.
turns.zh: 是的，这确实是一种夸张的观点，但我认为对于所有从零到一的创新项目来说，这一点尤为重要。如果你是一款独立应用的产品经理，身处大型公司内部，你就应该负责设计产品的层级结构、界面元素、交互流程等方方面面。虽然最终可能需要由技术设计师进行优化，但创意的核心始终在于你自己——毕竟产品成败取决于这些细节，就像消费类产品一样，这一切都由你来把控。所以在处理大型增长项目时，你或许可以适当降低对细节的关注度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. Okay, before we move on to the next phase of your journey of starting Gas, I heard there's an interesting story around where you were actually put within the Facebook office physically, where your team was put. Is there something there?
turns.zh: 我很赞同这个建议。好的，在我们进入创立Gas项目的下一阶段之前，我听说你们在Facebook办公室的具体位置挺有意思的，能跟我们讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. When we joined the new product experimentation group, we were actually seated I think at basically the same desk as Mark Zuckerberg. And that was pretty cool to see how the machine runs from Zuck's view. But we had a few artifacts that we had kept with us from our old office when we were running tbh, and one of them was this kind of pop art painting that I bought on the street when I needed to get something on the walls for our office. And it was this giant painting of Tim Cook. We had been carrying it between our orgs at Facebook just because it was a funny painting. And I kind of got it because it was kind of symbolic of who actually controls our destiny, is Apple. And so when we relocated to the area where Zuck was sitting, I put up the painting on the wall and it was basically a giant painting of Tim Cook was overlooking Zuck. And eventually one of the EAs there said, "Actually, do you think you could take that home?" And it kind of made sense because you can't really have a painting of another big tech executive overlooking us.
turns.zh: 是的。当我们加入新产品实验团队时，我们的办公桌位置和马克·扎克伯格几乎是同一排的。能从扎克伯格的视角观察整个团队运作机制，感觉很酷。不过我们从之前负责Tbh项目的旧办公室带了一些纪念品，其中有一幅我在街上买的波普艺术画，当时急需装饰办公室。画的是蒂姆·库克的巨幅肖像。我们在Facebook内部各个部门之间带着这幅画，因为它太有趣了。我买这幅画的初衷是想象性地表达，真正掌控我们命运的是苹果公司。所以当我们搬到扎克伯格的办公区时，我把这幅画挂在墙上，结果蒂姆·库克的巨幅肖像正俯瞰着扎克伯格。最后Facebook的行政助理问：“能不能把这幅画带回家？”这倒也说得通，毕竟让另一家科技巨头的CEO肖像俯瞰我们总归不太合适。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does it look like? Do you happen to have it?
turns.zh: 这幅画长什么样？你还留着吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah, I actually do. Let me go grab it.
turns.zh: 留着呢。我去拿一下。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Oh, wow. That's artistic. So that's Tim Cook. What is the idea there that he's peeking through this darkness staring at you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。哦，哇。这真有艺术感。所以那就是蒂姆·库克。他盯着你穿过黑暗的那种眼神，到底想表达什么？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. He's the real boss of all of us.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。他才是我们所有人的真正老大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see why Zuck would not want that staring at him all day. That's amazing. And I like that you still have that with you.
turns.zh: 我能理解扎克伯格为什么不想整天被那种目光盯着。太厉害了。而且我很高兴你还留着那个纪念品。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. One of the artifacts of that chapter of life. So good.
turns.zh: 是啊。这是那段人生经历留下的珍贵遗物。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So that was your Facebook journey, those four years. That's wild. You left Facebook. At some point, you started, I remember this, you started tweeting like, "Hey, I'm working on new app." Everyone was going nuts. "What are you working on?" And at this point, I think you probably in your mind thought, I am this one-hit wonder, I haven't shown that I can do this again and again. And so I think you probably have this motivation. Maybe talk about that, just like this drive of like, hey, I want to do this again. Is that where your mind was at?
turns.zh: 好的。所以这就是你四年的Facebook历程。真是太不可思议了。你离开了Facebook。我记得当时你开始在推特上发消息，比如“嘿，我正在开发新应用。”大家都炸锅了。“你在做什么？” 那时候，你心里可能在想，我只是昙花一现，还没证明自己能一次又一次成功。所以我觉得你当时应该有种动力，或许可以谈谈那种渴望再次成功的驱动力。这是你的真实想法吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: When that meme started, my intent was to start a venture-backed company and build something that would scale to be a big team and this durable thing that lasted many years and everything. And so I just made post that I was leaving Facebook and looking for some teammates. And I shared a couple of ideas with some people privately and there were some really crazy ideas that I shared. I'm not going to get into them, but then people started posting, "Oh my God, I just saw Nikita's app. It's crazy." And what happened was others saw that and then they started memeing it and it became this massive meme where they're like, "Oh, I just tried Nikita's app, it saved my marriage. Oh, I just quit drinking. My kids returned home after all these like," and it turned into this massive meme. And at the time, I didn't even have an app or anything. I wasn't even planning to launch it. It wasn't even an app, some of the ideas I was looking at. And so it just turned into this viral moment. I wasn't even committed to starting another company at that point. This was an exploration process. (00:55:48): But what happened was the market had crashed shortly thereafter, there was kind of the end of the Zerb era. The Fed started hiking rates. I think my portfolio was down like 30% or something and I was like, "Damn, this sucks. Maybe I should think about how to make money today." That's the reason we're in startups is to make money. And so there was always in the back of my head this question that I had, which was what if we had monetized tbh? Because the number one support message we received was can I pay to reveal who sent me polls? It was the number one question. And it was like, would it have made even more than the acquisition if we just monetized it? And I'm like, we could probably build this pretty fast, like probably in a month, month or two. Ended up being a lot longer, but we started rebuilding it. It was a new team. It was one of the engineers from a company called Paparazzi. His name's Zay Turner, and he started building it in my house and we had tested it to see would this new version of tbh actually resonate with kids five years later? That was actually the thing I wanted to know most of all was like would an anonymous polling app actually still be relevant five years later? And so we dropped it into the school just the same way I've always done it in-
turns.zh:
那个梗刚兴起的时候，我的初衷是创办一家风投支持的公司，打造一个能发展壮大、经久不衰的团队。我当时发了一条动态，宣布离开Facebook，寻找团队成员。私下里我和一些人分享了几个疯狂的创意，这里就不细说了。结果人们开始留言：“天哪，我刚看到Nikita的应用，太疯狂了！”其他人看到后，开始模仿这个梗，最终形成了一个大规模的网络现象。人们纷纷发帖说：“哦，我刚试用了Nikita的应用，挽救了我的婚姻。哦，我戒酒成功了。我的孩子回家了……”这样的例子层出不穷。当时我甚至还没有开发应用，也没打算正式推出。那些创意想法只是我探索阶段的构想。结果这个梗突然爆火。我那时甚至没想过再创办公司，这只是个探索过程。

（00:55:48）但随后市场崩盘，Zerb时代结束，美联储开始加息。我的投资组合暴跌30%左右，我当时想：“该死，这太糟了。或许我该想办法当下赚钱。”毕竟我们做创业就是为了赚钱。于是我脑海中始终有个疑问：如果我们当时把tbh货币化会怎样？因为用户最常提到的需求就是“能花钱查看发送匿名投票的人吗？”这几乎是头号痛点。如果直接变现，是否比被收购更值钱？我觉得我们大概能在一两个月内快速完成。但最终耗时更久，不过我们还是重新开发了新版本。新团队成员是来自Paparazzi公司的工程师Zay Turner，他在我家开始开发。我们测试新版本，看看五年后匿名投票应用是否还能吸引年轻人。这才是我最想知道的——匿名投票应用五年后还能有市场吗？于是我们还是像往常一样在学校试水——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was it the Georgia School again?
turns.zh: 又是在乔治亚州的学校吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yes, actually. We launched at the exact same school that we launched tbh on the exact same day five years later, in fact. And people sent a lot of messages, but it wasn't growing. So let me pedal back here a bit. So tbh grew through variety of things, people sharing their messages to Snapchat and text invites, and that was 2017. And the way you invited your friends on tbh was that you tap their name, your contact name, and there was a button that said Invite and then we used Twilio to send them a text message. And the regulatory environment actually had changed a lot over those five years. You really can't send texts from a server anymore. It has to be sent from the user's device. And just the point of clarification is a lot of people clone tbh over the years and they think that when you voted on people in the polls, it sent them a text. We never did that. That's egregiously illegal to do and also unethical at a user experience level to send texts when people don't even know what's happening. (00:58:57): But anyway, we couldn't send texts over Twilio anymore, and that led to people not sending as many invites when we created Gas because they had to pop the Compose window and hit Send. They're going to just tap Invite on five names. So we actually had to reinvent all the growth systems and it took about I think like nine launches including renaming the app, including features that just never existed on tbh. So it was actually just in many ways like yeah, the concept on the surface was the same, but it was very much a zero to one development cycle of figuring out how to grow this thing again in this climate.
turns.zh: 是的，事实上。五年后，我们在同一天、同一个学校推出了tbh。这次推出的结果令人失望，尽管人们发了很多消息，但用户增长却停滞不前。让我再回顾一下当时的情况。tbh的推广主要通过多种方式实现，比如用户将消息分享到Snapchat、通过短信邀请好友等，这一切都发生在2017年。当时邀请好友的方式是点击对方的姓名、自己的联系人姓名，点击“邀请”按钮后，系统会通过Twilio向对方发送短信。然而，五年间监管环境发生了巨大变化，现在已不再允许通过服务器发送短信，必须由用户设备直接发送。此外，需要特别说明的是，过去多年来许多模仿tbh的应用误导用户以为在投票环节发送短信给被投票者，但我们从未实施过这种行为。这不仅严重违反法律，从用户体验角度来看，在用户毫不知情的情况下发送短信也是不道德的。（00:58:57）不过由于无法再通过Twilio发送短信，导致用户在开发Gas时发送邀请的效率大打折扣——用户需要手动打开“撰写短信”界面并点击发送，而之前只需点击五个联系人的“邀请”按钮即可。因此，我们不得不彻底重建整个增长体系，历经约九次迭代，包括更改应用名称、添加tbh从未有过的功能。总之，表面上概念相似，但在当前的环境下，这其实是一次从零到一的全新开发周期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that point is really important to you. I think a lot of people are like Nikita just sold the same app twice. What a guy. And the point you're making here is not only was the infrastructure completely different, the team was different, you had to rethink the entire flywheel of how it worked and how it grew.
turns.zh: 我知道这一点对你来说很重要。我觉得很多人会觉得尼基塔不过是把同一款应用卖了两次，多牛啊。可你现在强调的重点是，不仅基础设施完全不同，团队也换了，而且你还得重新思考整个增长飞轮的运作机制和策略。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. And there were so many layers of like we validated one thing and then the next thing we got stuck on. Like, okay, people send a lot of messages. Cool, great. The next thing was will it spread within a school? That took us a while to get right. Will it hop schools? Each of those was a very, very challenging problem in light of the new climate that we were operating in. And I always do things by the book when it comes to operating legally within the compliance framework. And that's something when I meet founders and they tell me some growth thing that they're doing, and I'm like, "You can't do that. That's going to cause way more trouble down the line. It's going to burn users too." And so we always wanted to make it abundantly clear how our growth system, how you are inviting friends and all that. You can kind of go on a whole diatribe on that because the thing that I see a lot of founders do is they in the background use user data in ways that it shouldn't be used. They invite people on your behalf and all that. (01:01:21): And I have this kind of crazy view that the internet is this living and breathing thing. There's Wikipedia article called the Gaia Hypothesis, which is about biology. And it's basically like the earth is kind of living and breathing and can respond to threats. Okay? And when you enter the rainforest too deep, Ebola virus will be released. Okay? So I think the internet operates on a similar paradigm here where if you do the wrong thing by users, the internet will come back and get even and defend itself. And so whenever I design products, I try to do right by users because it'll always come back much worse and I think you should always operate above board with how you design your growth systems. And with Gas, we had to do things the right way and we had to figure out at each particular moment or problem that we solve, will it spread within schools? Will it hop schools? Will people pay for it? All of these things was a whole reinvention of the original product.
turns.zh:
是的。我们遇到了很多层层叠叠的难题。比如，我们验证了一个功能，接着又卡在下一个环节。就比如，用户发送大量消息，这没问题。但学校内的传播问题却让我们花了不少时间才解决。再比如，用户跨校传递信息，这又是一个挑战。鉴于当时我们所处的监管环境，每个问题都极具挑战性。在合规框架内合法运营时，我向来循规蹈矩。当我遇到创业者时，他们会跟我说一些不靠谱的增长策略，我就会提醒他们：“你不能这么做，这会带来长期麻烦，还会损害用户利益。” 因此，我们始终清晰传达我们的增长机制，比如邀请好友等功能。关于这部分，你可以展开详细阐述，因为我发现很多创业者会背地里利用用户数据，比如替用户发送邀请信息等。  

我有个疯狂的观点：互联网是一个有生命力的存在。维基百科上有篇叫《盖亚假说》的生物学文章，提到地球有自我修复的能力。如果你过度开发雨林，埃博拉病毒就会被释放出来。所以我认为互联网也有类似的机制——如果你伤害了用户，互联网会反击自卫。因此，我设计产品时始终以用户利益为先，因为错误行为会反噬回来。Gas 项目中，我们必须确保每项功能都合规：学校内传播吗？跨校传播吗？用户会付费吗？这些问题都迫使我们彻底重构原有产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you shared that because I think a lot of people see you from the outside and they think you're doing all kinds of these skeezy growth hacks and making teens do things that aren't really mentally healthy for them. But it's clear that that's the opposite of how you think about it, that you're trying to stay very positive, like you only allow positive communication. You do things that as you just said, are going to be good long-term, the internet's not going to come and try to shut you down.
turns.zh: 很高兴你能分享这些心得。我发现很多人从外部看你时，认为你在玩各种不道德的增长技巧，让青少年沉溺于不健康的内容。但很显然，你的理念恰恰相反——你致力于营造积极的生态，比如只允许正向交流。正如你所说，这些长期策略最终会带来回报，互联网也不会因此封杀你们。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: The point you bring up here about wanting to build a positive thing, some people, sometimes I get criticism. It's not actually that often, but they say, "Oh, you're building an app that makes teens feeling insecure or anything." But with Gas, I think we received a message every single day from a user telling us that they reconsidered suicide or other forms of self-harm. The app sent you positive messages and affirmations. It made teens feel really good. And I think that is lost on a lot of people. Instagram can make you feel jealousy and a lot of other social networks are a mixed bag in terms of impact. But we were entirely focused on making teens feel better. (01:03:49): And some people might say, "Oh, what if someone doesn't get voted for something?" We actually built a system to ensure everyone got a vote. And what we did was we put your name in polls at a higher frequency if you weren't being voted on recently. So we wanted to spread the love in every way possible, and that's what really motivated me to grow this thing was watching how it was impacting 10 million kids in such a short period of time.
turns.zh: 你在这里提到的想要建立积极事物这一观点，确实有人批评我。但这种情况并不常见，他们会说：“哦，你开发的这个应用会让青少年感到不安，或者带来其他负面影响。” 但就Gas这款应用而言，我认为我们每天都会收到用户的反馈，称他们重新考虑了自杀或其他自残行为。应用会向用户发送积极的信息和肯定语句，让青少年感觉良好。但我觉得很多人并没有意识到这一点。Instagram会让人产生嫉妒心理，其他社交网络在影响力方面也是好坏参半。但我们完全专注于让青少年感觉更好。（01:03:49）：有些人可能会问：“哦，如果有人没被投票选中怎么办？” 我们实际上建立了一个系统，确保每个人都能获得投票机会。如果你最近没有被投票，我们会更频繁地将你的名字纳入投票选项。所以我们想尽一切办法传递正能量，而真正激励我发展这个项目的，是看到它在如此短的时间内影响了1000万青少年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really appreciate you adding that. I didn't know all those things about the way you thought about these apps. Interestingly, I don't know how much you can go into this, but there is a lot of stuff going on with Gas around human trafficking and all this stuff where people thought people were being kidnapped through Gas, which is yeah, talk about that whatever you can because that's pretty crazy.
turns.zh: 我真的很感激你补充了这些信息。我之前并不知道你对这些应用的看法这么深入。有趣的是，我不知道你能透露多少细节，但Gas应用在打击人口贩卖方面确实存在很多问题，比如人们以为通过Gas被绑架之类的。如果你方便的话，能否谈谈这些情况？这真的太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: We had this hoax started where people were saying the app was used for human trafficking. And I was like, "This is so strange." This is a anonymous polling app without messaging and the only thing you could do is send compliments to your friends. And I researched into it and I saw that this is actually plaguing a lot of apps and any app that has gone viral in any way has actually had this hoax started. And part of the reason it happens is it gets you attention if you say that about an app. As a teenager, if you say, "Oh, this app is dangerous," and then you get a bunch of followers and who doesn't love followers? So it's actually a really viral piece of content if you put it out. And so we had this hoax started and we were like, "This could kill the company." And I talked to a bunch of founders that it happened to them and they said, "Yeah, we had to shut down because of that."
turns.zh: 当时有一起骗局，说这款应用被用于人口贩卖。我当时就觉得：“这太奇怪了。” 这是一款匿名投票应用，没有聊天功能，你唯一能做的事就是给朋友发送赞美。我调查后发现，这种情况困扰着很多应用，任何走红的应用都会遭遇这种骗局。这种骗局之所以能传播，部分原因是如果你这样说某个应用，能吸引眼球。作为青少年，你如果说：“哦，这个应用很危险。”就能收获一堆粉丝，谁不喜欢粉丝呢？所以这种内容一旦传播出去，就会迅速走红。我们当时也遭遇了这种骗局，觉得“这可能会毁了公司”。我和很多创始人聊过，他们也遇到过这种情况，他们说：“是啊，因为这个我们不得不关闭公司了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: And I was like, "Is this it? Is this the end of the company?" And I remember it hit number one when we started getting a few of these reports in our support channels. And I was like, "I'm just going to plant the flag on posts that we hit number one in the App Store because this thing's probably going to shut down soon." So I make this announcement on Twitter, "I just made the number one app and I thought it would just be dead in a week." And then I just had this sudden burst of energy and I was like, "I'm going to win. I'm going to fight this. This is not true. It makes no sense at all." (01:06:20): And so we fought it at every vector possible, this completely made up hoax. We met with journalists, reporters to make sure that the number one match every time you search Gas app human trafficking was Gas app is not for human trafficking. And so that ended up being The Washington Post headline. We insisted that that be the headline if we do the interview. So that was the first thing that showed up on Google anytime someone searched it. There were schools and even a police station that posted that this app is used for human trafficking. I called those superintendents, I called those police chiefs and have got them to publicly retract it. And we had some of the reviews on the App Store. We asked Apple to remove them because we got review bombed. (01:07:07): But the thing that actually was the most impactful was my girlfriend made a video, a TikTok video explaining that it's not true. And anytime someone deleted their account, they could watch this video explaining it's not true. And at the peak, we had 3% of users deleting their accounts per day. So it was like a catastrophe for an app and we got it down to 0.1% through relentless, relentless effort. And it was really just an unusual thing that happens when you grow really fast is this human trafficking hoax that starts. And you don't understand how crazy it is until it happens to your company, but it was kind of hilarious to think about. This app was the most harmless benign thing you could think of.
turns.zh: 我当时就想：“这就是结局吗？公司就这么完了？”记得当我们开始在支持渠道收到这些负面报道时，应用登上榜首的那一刻。我当时就说：“我要在帖子里标注我们登上App Store榜首了，因为这应用可能很快就要关门了。”于是我在推特上发文：“我刚登上榜首，结果一周后它就被封了。” 然后我突然来了股劲头：“我要赢，我要反击，这完全是无稽之谈！” （01:06:20）：于是我们从各个方面展开反击，针对这个完全虚构的骗局。我们与记者、媒体见面，确保每次搜索“Gas app 人口贩卖”时，结果都显示“Gas app并非用于人口贩卖”。最终《华盛顿邮报》用这句话作为标题。我们坚持在采访中必须使用这个标题，这样用户在谷歌搜索时就能看到正确信息。甚至有学校和警察局声称该应用用于人口贩卖。我联系了那些校长和警局负责人，让他们公开撤回指控。我们还删除了App Store上的负面评论，因为遭遇了恶意差评攻击。（01:07:07）：但最有效的应对措施是我的女友制作了一段TikTok视频，解释事实并非如此。每当用户删除账号时，他们都能看到这段辟谣视频。高峰时期，每天有3%的用户删除账号。这对应用来说简直是灾难，但通过不懈努力，我们最终将这一比例降至0.1%。这类因快速发展而引发的虚假指控，实在令人费解。直到亲身经历时，才会意识到其疯狂程度，但回想起来倒也觉得滑稽。这款应用本是市面上最无害、最良性的存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is insane. I did not know this full story. And you were doing all this while you were trying to scale the app and trying to keep the servers up and try to grow it, right? What was that like to try to manage all these things at once?
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。我之前完全不知道整个事件的全貌。你当时一边要应对这些危机，一边还要努力推广应用、维护服务器正常运转，对吧？同时处理这么多事情，压力得多大啊？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I was sleeping three hours a day for three months. It was extraordinarily difficult to do it all. Our team was also relentless though. They would come over to my house 9:00 a.m. stay until midnight and just do that seven days a week. So yeah, it was definitely one of the most physically draining things ever, but we were just so tactical. I remember investors were asking to meet with us and I said, "If you can't get a celebrity to post that this isn't true, then we're not interested." But yeah, we went after it on every vector and it ended up being okay.
turns.zh: 那三个月我每天只睡三个小时。想把所有事情都处理到位实在太难了。不过我们的团队非常敬业。他们每天早上9点就到我家，晚上12点才走，每周七天如此。确实是身体上最消耗精力的一段经历，但我们策略得当。我记得投资者找我们见面时，我说：“如果你们找不到名人发声辟谣，那我们没兴趣。”不过最终我们全方位出击，总算渡过难关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how you took your brain to this other completely different problem and thought about all the levers you could use to change the conversation around the app.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你能跳出固有思维，针对应用舆情的各个维度想出应对之策。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. I remember we had these TikTok videos that were made that were saying it was true and I networked my way all the way to the CEO of TikTok and I said, "Can you delete these?" And we got this information deleted. Yeah, so it was really a whole new test of our team's capacities was fighting. The key thing that you have to know though when you have a hoax spreading about your app is you really have to make sure the hoax is less viral than your app. And at a few points, the hoax was more viral than our app and we had to take this-
turns.zh: 是的。我记得我们制作了那些TikTok视频，声称这些内容是真实的。我通过关系网联系到了TikTok的CEO，问他：“你能删掉这些视频吗？”最终这些信息被删除了。是的，这确实是对我们团队能力的一次全新考验。当你的应用被虚假信息传播时，关键是要确保虚假信息的传播速度比你的应用更慢。在某些时候，虚假信息的传播速度甚至超过了我们的应用，我们不得不采取措施——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The K-factor of the hoax.
turns.zh: 虚假信息的K因子。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's absurd. Okay. So broadly, you built this app. Again, a big success. I saw a stat that you made $11 million in sales through the app, 10 million downloads. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太离谱了。好的。总的来说，你开发了这款应用。这又是一个巨大的成功。我看到一项数据，显示通过这款应用实现了1100万美元的销售额，下载量达1000万次。对吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. It was a blowout success in terms of like it grew bigger than tbh. We monetized it. We ran almost entirely on startup credits, so it was basically-
turns.zh: 是的。它取得了惊人的成功，甚至比tbh更受欢迎。我们通过它实现了变现。整个团队几乎完全依靠初创公司的资金支持，所以基本上——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like Cloud Credits? Like AWS Credits?
turns.zh: 比如云计算积分？亚马逊云服务（AWS）积分？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. AWS Credits, Mixpanel. I remember when I saw the early data, I'm like, "Okay, now it's time for me to negotiate every bill down to the last cent of margin for every vendor." And I got credits everywhere, and so we really were tactical with that. And so we ended up being all just pure cashflow for the team. We had no investors. And it was just so interesting though that the way that I started posting about it on Twitter was it kind of captured the zeitgeist of the internet. And we didn't intend on selling it. We were just going to let this thing run its course and just be this app that kind of lives in the background of our lives. But once it started capturing the zeitgeist of Twitter, I was like, "Wait a minute, we could probably sell this thing." And that's when we started engaging with some of these, we ended up getting three companies that wanted to buy it. I won't be able to say them, but ultimately we ended up selling to Discord and we joined Discord.
turns.zh: 是的。AWS积分、Mixpanel数据分析平台。我记得看到早期数据时，我想：“好吧，现在是时候为每个供应商把每分钱的利润都压到最低了。” 我成功争取到了各处的优惠，所以我们在这方面做得很灵活。最终，整个团队完全依靠现金流运营。我们没有投资者。然而有趣的是，我最初在Twitter上分享这款应用时，它恰好抓住了互联网的时代精神。我们原本没打算出售它，只是想让它自然发展，让它成为一款默默存在于我们生活背景中的应用。但当它开始引发Twitter用户的共鸣时，我意识到：“等等，我们或许可以把它卖掉。” 于是我们开始与一些公司接洽，最终有三家公司有意收购。我不能透露他们的名字，但最终我们把它卖给了Discord，并加入了Discord团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So before we move on to the next part of the journey and some of the other insights that I want to get into, is there any lasting lessons that you took away from Gas as a product that you take with you to advising startups in terms of building the product design? I know there's many, but any that stand out most that you think are really interesting to share?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在我们进入旅程的下一阶段，探讨我希望深入探讨的其他见解之前，你从Gas这款产品中获得了哪些持久的经验教训，可以应用于为初创公司提供产品设计方面的建议吗？我知道有很多，但有没有最突出的、你认为值得分享的？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I think I kind of touched on this before, which was trying to validate things in a sequence of like, will people use the core flow? Will people spread it within their peer group? Will it hop peer groups? And what I think the most important thing that I learned is that's actually a really great way to do zero to one product development is execute at 100% for the thing you're trying to validate at that specific stage of the product development cycle. And then you can kind of half-ass the rest just so you can get 100% signal on that one part. (01:12:25): And so we made the polling experience just perfect. The questions were great. Push notifications, everything worked. And then the next stage was getting sharing and virality working. And so compartmentalizing those things because ultimately you'll have too much scope creep if you try to solve everything at once and validate. And also you're not going to get signal too, like you're trying to test one thing at a time. So the way that now I approach a lot of consumer product development is if this is true, then what next needs to be true for this thing to work out? And these layers of conditional statements. And the more layers you have, the higher risk your product is, so you should try to condense it to about like four things that must be true for the thing to work.
turns.zh: 我觉得我之前已经提过这个观点了，那就是尝试验证一系列假设：比如，用户会使用核心功能吗？他们会在同龄人中传播这款产品吗？产品会跨越不同用户群体吗？而我学到的最重要的一点是，在产品开发的特定阶段，100%的专注于验证当前阶段的关键假设，实际上是实现从0到1产品开发的绝佳方式。这样一来，你就能在其他方面保持低标准，但仍能在关键环节获得100%的反馈。（01:12:25）：所以我们把投票体验做到尽善尽美。问题设计得很棒，推送通知功能也完美运行。接下来要解决的是如何实现分享和病毒式传播。因此，我将这些功能分开处理，因为如果你试图一次性解决所有问题并进行验证，最终会面临过度范围蔓延的风险。同时，由于每次只测试一个假设，你也更容易获得清晰的反馈。因此，我现在开发消费级产品的思路是：如果当前假设成立，那么下一步需要满足哪些条件才能让产品成功？然后层层递进地设置条件语句。层数越多，产品的风险就越高，所以要尽量将条件简化到四个关键要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this comes back to your advice of the thing you need to get good at is testing and learning and making it really quick.
turns.zh: 这又回到了你的建议——你需要擅长快速测试、学习和迭代。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Maybe one last thing along this thread. I'm just really curious how this hoax came to be, like who's behind it? How does this happen?
turns.zh: 好的。或许最后再补充一点关于这次事件的思考。我真的很好奇这个骗局是如何产生的，幕后黑手是谁？又是如何蔓延开来的？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: We got a original support message, which was a screenshot of a story on Snapchat and it said, "Do not download the Gas app. It's for human trafficking." Okay? And it was a screenshot that had like that mirror effect where you have like 10 people that screenshotted it. More, like 40 people because it had all the usernames. So I was looking at this and I'm like, "How many people have seen this?" And it looked like a viral thing on Snapchat. And then I went to the App Store page and I saw a review that said this app is for human trafficking. And I went to my team and I said, "This will probably kill the company. This will kill the product. I've seen this before with consumer apps and it's evident to me this is going to be 10 times bigger tomorrow." And they were like, "No. It's just one message. What do you mean?" I'm like, "No, no, it's been screenshotted 40 times and now it's on the App Store page." And we got another message four hours later. (01:14:35): And the next day, it was our entire App Store page was just covered with reviews saying that the app's for human trafficking. And we actually had to rebrand the app. We relaunched it once and we're like, "Let's just call it something different. Just relaunch it on the other side of the country." We did that, started going viral again. And the craziest-
turns.zh: 我们最初收到一条支持请求，是Snapchat上一个故事的截图，内容写着：“不要下载Gas应用，它用于人口贩卖。” 好吗？截图带有那种镜像效果，显示有10个人截图了这张图，可能还有40个人截图了，因为上面列出了所有用户名。我看着这张截图，心想：“有多少人看到过这个？”看起来这在Snapchat上像个病毒式传播的帖子。然后我去App Store页面，看到一条评论说这个应用是用于人口贩卖的。我找团队说：“这可能会毁了公司，毁了产品。我之前见过这种情况在消费类应用中发生，显然明天情况会更糟。” 他们说：“不，这只是一条评论。你什么意思？” 我说：“不不不，它被截图了40次，现在App Store页面上到处都是这样的评论。” 四个小时后我们又收到另一条消息。（01:14:35）：第二天，整个App Store页面都被指责该应用用于人口贩卖的评论淹没了。我们不得不重塑品牌，重新上线一次，然后决定改个名字，在另一个地区重新发布。我们这样做后，又开始迅速走红。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: ... again. And the craziest thing was it re-emerged and what happened was one user was friends with another person in another state and they got an invitation. And that user told them, "Oh, that was in my state. It's actually for human trafficking." And then it just completely started again and then it was too late at that point to relaunch again. We just realized, " We got to fight this thing." And ultimately, I don't think we'll ever know the true origin, but it was definitely a living, breathing like hoax.
turns.zh: 又来了。最疯狂的是，它再次死灰复燃。当时有个用户和另一个州的朋友互加好友，结果收到邀请。那个用户告诉他：“哦，这是我们州的骗局，实际上是用来贩卖人口的。” 然后整个骗局又卷土重来，那时再想重新上线已经太晚了。我们意识到，必须彻底对抗这个问题。虽然我们可能永远无法查明其真实来源，但这绝对是个持续发酵的骗局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is insane. The story just gets more and more interesting. What were some of the previous names, by the way? Is that something you can share?
turns.zh: 这太不可思议了。整个故事越来越精彩。顺便问一下，这个应用之前用过哪些名字？能透露一下吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah, we went through a bunch. One of them was called Crush, one of them was called Melt, and another was... The interesting thing about Crush is we got a great domain. We thought this would be the name. This was between some of the re-brands. We tested it and we saw that invitations dropped significantly under the Crush name and we were like, "What's going on here?" And we found that actually when you invite someone to an app, regardless of the app, you generally... Boys invite boys, girls invite girls to apps. And boys didn't want to invite their friends to an app called Crush with a pink icon. (01:16:35): And then we looked at the data and the app. I mean this was true TBH too, which was the app indexed about 60 to 65% women. So we were just like, "Let's make the app more masculine and see what happens. We need balance on this." So we made the icon black with a flame, called it Gas and the invites rate jumped. And you think a name doesn't matter, but right at the moment of sending an invite... So that was one of the interesting insights on the naming process.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们换了好几个名字。其中一个叫Crush，一个叫Melt，还有一个……Crush这个名字特别有意思。我们本来有个很棒的域名，觉得应该用这个名字。当时正处于品牌重塑阶段。我们测试后发现Crush这个名字下的邀请量急剧下降，我们就开始思考：“这是怎么回事？” 结果发现，无论哪个应用，邀请好友时都是“男生邀请男生，女生邀请女生”。而男生根本不想用带粉色图标的Crush邀请好友。（01:16:35）我们分析了数据和应用指标，发现Crush里60%到65%的用户都是女性。所以我们决定让应用更男性化，看看效果如何。于是我们把图标改成黑色火焰图案，改名为Gas，结果邀请率立马提升了。你可能觉得名字无关紧要，但在发送邀请的那一刻……这就是命名过程中的一个深刻洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, there's just endless stories that we could keep getting into, but we've also gone very long, so I'm going to try to move on to another topic. So I ask people on Twitter what to ask you? Just that question got a thousand likes just me asking, "What should I ask Nikita?" And the most common question, I'm sure you get this a lot, is just people wondering, do you ever want to build a durable consumer app? Is it possible to build a durable consumer app? (01:17:30): Scott Belsky asked this, Robert at Figma asked this, and Scott actually had a really nice way of describing it about why are so many quick sensation consumer apps proving to be more akin to summer songs than enduring standalone products and businesses? So there's kind of two questions here. One is, do you aim to build a durable consumer app? And two, how possible is it?
turns.zh: 天啊，还有无数故事可以聊，但时间有限，我得转到下一个话题了。我在Twitter上问大家想问什么问题，就我问“该问尼基塔什么？”这条问答就收获了上千个赞。最常见的问题（相信你也经常被问）是，用户想知道你是否想打造持久的消费级应用？这是否可行？（01:17:30）斯科特·贝尔斯基、Figma的罗伯特都问过这个问题。斯科特用了一个很棒的比喻，解释为什么很多快速蹿红的消费级应用更像夏日金曲，而非经久不衰的产品和企业。这里有两个问题：一、你是否致力于打造持久的消费级应用？二、这有多大可能性？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: A lot of the fundamental tools for communicating with our friends either messaging or broadcasting one-to-many like on stories or the incumbents have built pretty large motes in terms of network effects and to provide true an order of magnitude better experience is non-trivial because they've been actually improving these products so much over the years and there's not that many entry points. (01:18:31): Not to say that it's not impossible. Snapchat was showed that there was style of messaging that people wanted that the incumbents weren't serving. But I think there's these kind of edges that you can go after with a much higher probability of success and they might not actually be something that's durable necessarily. And I think finding durability for a communication or social product, that's a black swan event. Retention for consumer social is there's a tremendous amount of randomness. There's one every decade. If it was simple, I would just be printing $1 trillion companies. (01:19:15): I be printing Facebook's every time I sat down. But I think it's actually a lot of it is pure randomness. On the other hand, growing a product can be a science. With certainty, if you're good at your job, you can make an app grow and go viral. Now why haven't I tried to take the viral part and build something that has been durable or long-lasting? I'll tell you a little bit about my motivations. My favorite part about product development is you make this thing through the night. You build it and you watch it take over the internet. (01:19:54): That is the most thrilling drug I think you could ever experience. And just watching it spread all over the country is like you drop an app in the deep south in Georgia and then you look on your analytics dashboard and 40% of the high school down your street in Los Angeles has downloaded it one week later. That's a really profound feeling. It's crazy to have that sort of impact as a three-person team, and I live for that. (01:20:26): When I joined Facebook, here's an interesting connection. So I joined Facebook and I saw that many of my peers were looking up to VPs and they're like, "That's what I want to make it to one day. I want to run a large organization. I want to have lots of reports." And then I met with VPs and they were actually jealous of me because my quality of life was actually pretty cool. I got to build something high impact that made many teens feel better about themselves, made a decent amount of money. And then I wasn't in charge of this becoming a people manager that has to run this large organization for many years. (01:21:11): I think one day I will run maybe a venture scale business, but I will say that I kind of like the way that I've been doing things so far in terms of quality of life and being fun. Financially, it's been great. So I think that part is what motivates me. And yeah, I don't think running a large corporation is necessarily what I described as fun.
turns.zh: 许多与朋友交流的基本工具——无论是即时通讯还是一对多的信息分享（比如故事功能）——都已被现有巨头牢牢占据，形成了强大的网络效应。要想提供真正比现有水平高出一个数量级的体验并非易事，因为这些产品多年来一直在不断优化，而且切入点实在不多。（01:18:31）：这并不是说这完全不可能。Snapchat就证明了，人们渴望一种现有巨头未能提供的信息传递方式。但我认为这类突破性创新需要更高的成功概率，而它们未必能持久。我认为打造一款持久的通信或社交产品堪称黑天鹅事件。消费者社交产品的留存率存在巨大随机性，每十年才会出现一次这样的机会。如果这很简单，我就能随随便便创造出万亿美元级别的公司了。（01:19:15）：但实际上这很大程度上是纯粹的随机性。另一方面，产品增长可以是一门科学。只要你擅长本职工作，就能让应用实现增长并走红。那么为什么我没有尝试抓住病毒式传播的机遇，打造一款持久的产品呢？让我稍微谈谈我的动机。我最喜欢的产品开发环节，就是通宵打造一款产品，看着它征服整个互联网。（01:19:54）：这恐怕是人能体验到的最令人兴奋的感觉。看着它在全国蔓延，就像在乔治亚州南部发布一款应用，然后在分析仪表板上看到洛杉矶街头40%的高中生一周后就下载了它。这真是令人震撼的感觉。作为一个三人团队能产生这样的影响力简直不可思议，我为此而活。（01:20:26）：我加入Facebook时，发现了一个有趣的现象。许多同行都敬仰VP级别的高管，梦想着未来也能晋升到那个级别，管理一个大团队。但当我与VP们交流时，他们反倒对我心生羡慕，因为我的生活质量其实相当不错。我能打造出影响深远的产品，让许多青少年自我感觉良好，同时还能赚得不错的收入。而我无需承受多年管理大团队的压力，去当一个人民经理。（01:21:11）：我相信未来某天我会经营一家风险投资支持的企业，但目前我更享受现在的生活方式和工作的乐趣。从财务角度来看，这也很棒。所以这就是激励我的原因。说真的，我并不认为管理大公司一定有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing, man. I am really happy we went here. So much of this resonates with the way I think. And obviously, a big part of this is also just it's very hard, as you said, to build a consumer app that grows first of all. Second, that actually lasts. But that is interesting that you do hope to one day build a venture funded business.
turns.zh: 太棒了，老兄。真高兴我们聊了这些。很多观点都和我不谋而合。显然，正如你所说，打造一款能快速增长的消费者应用极其困难，而要让它真正持久更是难上加难。但你确实希望未来能创立一家获得风险投资支持的企业，这点很有意思。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I mean TBH was venture backed, but I just don't... I think I'm going to have to... Do I want to sign up for 10 years? And if you actually look at some of the numbers on the actual proceeds that some of these founders get after an IPO, after seven rounds of dilution, a lot of them are pretty comparable to what we get from our apps for 90 days of work. So yeah, the trade-offs there are pretty faithful.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，TBH（一个社交平台）确实获得了风险投资，但我就是不... 我觉得我可能得... 我要注册10年吗？如果你看看一些创始人在IPO后经过七轮稀释后实际获得的收益数字，很多都和我们开发一款应用90天就能赚到的钱相当。所以是啊，这其中的权衡还是挺现实的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually, just on that note, so what would make you actually decide to go venture funded? You talked about how if you're going more mainstream, non-teens folks after 22 years old, is that why you would go that route?
turns.zh: 说到这儿，到底是什么因素让你决定接受风险投资呢？你提到如果要面向主流用户群体，22岁以上非青少年用户群体，是不是这就是你选择这条路的原因？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: I don't think that it's necessarily that part. I think if I could keep the team lean and scale up... I think there's some actual founders that actually operate very lean teams and have reached very large scale in terms of the valuations of the company. Actually the most iconic example is Elon Musk. His teams are actually pretty thin overall and he's in the weeds doing product development. And so I think, yeah, if I was to ever do it, I would do it under very specific set of operating principles versus turning it into a big tech company.
turns.zh: 我觉得不一定是这个原因。我觉得如果能保持团队精简并实现规模化... 确实有一些创始人运营着精简团队，却在公司估值方面达到了极高的水平。最典型的例子就是埃隆·马斯克。他的团队整体规模很小，但他却埋头于产品开发。所以我觉得，如果我要走这条路，我会遵循一套非常明确的运营原则，而不是把公司做成大型科技公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Queue investor is emailing you right now with term sheets. Okay. Nikita, this has been amazing. There's one last segment I want to spend a little time on, which is just kind of a rapid fire of pieces of advice you've shared that I think is incredibly insightful about how to build a successful consumer app. And so I'm thinking I'll just go through three to five and see what you think and see what you can add to the advice. How does that sound?
turns.zh: 投资者现在正在发邮件给你送来投资条款。好的。尼基塔，感谢你的分享。最后我想花点时间快速总结一下你提到的建议，我觉得这些对打造成功的消费者应用非常有启发。所以我想先列出三到五条，看看你的看法，再补充一些建议。怎么样？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Sounds great.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So the first is just contact permissions in iOS 18 changes the game and how people can grow apps basically makes it harder to invite your friends. Thoughts on how people should be thinking about this in their products.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。所以第一条是iOS 18中的联系权限改革彻底改变了游戏规则，用户获取新用户的难度大大增加。你对开发者如何应对这个挑战有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: When I first saw it, I was really concerned.
turns.zh: 我第一次看到这个变化时，真的很担忧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw your tweet about it. You're like, "That's the end. Game over."
turns.zh: 我看到你发的推文，你说"这下完了。游戏结束了。"

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Just let me frame things up for you. The contact permissions screen, you average about 65% approval rate across all apps. It's higher for teens, lower for adults, but if you have a 65% consenting to contacts access, then the next step on this new iOS 18 change is you select which contacts you want to allow the app to access. And it's an alphabetical list. And that alphabetical list for me, I have 550 contacts or something. (01:24:55): The first 10 contacts are punctuation symbols from whatever dirty entry I put when I was driving or something. So you have to scroll down and find that name. So I have to find Lenny. I have to add you. And what if you're not an app user? So I just added you or three others. Assuming users are willing to even do that. You and then the three others never sign up, but maybe three of your friends do. (01:25:24): But I never get connected to them because there's no over... So my expectation is it's going to be very difficult to find friends on apps going forward to invite friends on apps going forward. And that founders will need to rethink how they do it. And of the companies, I'm working with on intro, we are looking at ways to reinvent what contact sync is or what purpose it served. It's not promising, but we have some good leads and I think we'll have a whole new set of apps emerging as a consequence. But if you're betting on contact sync as a company right now, you better start thinking about plan B.
turns.zh: 让我来给你解释一下。联系人权限界面显示，在所有应用中，平均约65%的用户会授予访问权限。青少年用户的同意率较高，成年用户则较低。但如果你有65%的用户同意应用访问联系人，那么iOS 18新政策的下一步就是让用户选择允许哪些联系人被访问。这份联系人列表是按字母顺序排列的。对我来说，列表里有550个联系人左右。（01:24:55）：前10个联系人是一些标点符号，可能是我开车时随手输入的乱码内容。所以你得往下翻才能找到那个名字。比如我要找Lenny，我得先把你加进去。那如果对方不是应用用户呢？我刚刚把你和另外三个人加进了，假设用户愿意这么做。但那三个人可能永远不会注册，而你的三个朋友可能会注册。（01:25:24）：但我永远无法与他们建立连接，因为没有……所以我预计未来在应用上寻找朋友、邀请朋友会变得非常困难。创始人们需要重新思考如何做这件事。在我合作的Intro公司，我们正在探索如何重塑联系人同步功能或重新定义其用途。这条路并不容易，但我们有一些好的思路，我认为未来会涌现出一批全新的应用。但如果你现在作为一家公司押注联系人同步功能，最好开始考虑B计划了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I take away here is just it is now much different and there's an opportunity to think of something really clever that would give you a huge advantage if you can crack it.
turns.zh: 所以我的理解是，现在情况已经大不相同了，这为那些能想出巧妙解决方案的人提供了机会，如果能成功开发，可能会带来巨大优势。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yes, but most likely I think most apps will not have social graphs going forward and this will entrench incumbents even more. I don't think Apple acknowledged that. I think the person that designed the feature probably has never built an app or done contact sync before because the flow is egregiously bad and it doesn't actually even, I think, benefit the user's privacy because it just completely eliminates the feature altogether.
turns.zh: 是的，但我认为大多数应用未来很可能不会再有社交图谱了，这会让现有巨头进一步巩固地位。我觉得苹果并未意识到这一点。设计这个功能的人可能从未开发过应用或做过联系人同步，因为整个流程糟糕透顶，而且实际上并不能真正保护用户隐私，因为这个功能完全被彻底废弃了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, next topic. So you helped this product called Dupe succeed. It's doing incredibly well from what I can see. And I saw you tweet about one of the key things that you helped them through, which is to invert, I'm reading this quote, "Inverting the time to value so that the user experience is the aha moment in seconds." Talk about that insight and how important that is to building a successful consumer social app.
turns.zh: 好的，下一个话题。你帮助过一个叫Dupe的产品取得成功。就我所见，它做得非常出色。我看到你发推文提到你帮助他们做的一个关键点，那就是反转时间与价值的关系，让用户体验在几秒钟内就能获得惊喜。能谈谈这个洞察吗？它对打造成功的消费级社交应用有多重要？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: This kind of concept of getting users to the aha moment is something I recurringly bring up to every company I work with. And you have to understand that in 2024, people's attention spans are like three seconds. It's really sad, but we are spread thin through so many notifications, products, everything that if you can't demonstrate value in the first three seconds, it's over. And this also leads back to the contact sync question that you talked about was you have to sign up and then the first night you have to see all of your friends on the app and experience it, otherwise you'll churn. (01:27:55): So this idea of inverting the value, when I was working with Dupe, they had this kind of shopping app that had a bunch of different features and there was one feature that I saw that was interesting called Deal Hop and it allowed you to just put in a product page and it would find the cheapest version of it online. Something I already do through a bunch of duct taped methods of Google image search, Google Lens. And I was like, "That should be a whole company. But how are we going to teach users to do it and how do we expose them to that aha moment as fast as possible in a memorable iconic way?" (01:28:38): I had this product I built a while back where you just type the domain in front of an existing URL. So I told them, "You should try this. It's very marketable, but you need to get a very short domain that matches what you're doing." And so he went out and bought Dupe.com for I don't know how much, but when he bought that I was pretty excited. I'm like, well, if this doesn't work, I'm going to feel terrible, but if it does work, it's going to be a blowout success. (01:29:05): So we put out a couple videos about it and then it was iconic, went viral, the videos. Users remembered to do it, to type dupe.com in front of a URL. Now I think they're making millions in ARR in a matter, and I think under 60 days of launching. And that was a blowout success. And of the companies I work with, I would say it happens about 50% of the time we hit that much success, but we hit success. I think 50% of the time it's outright failure because consumer is so random.
turns.zh: 这种让用户获得“啊哈时刻”的理念，是我反复向合作的每家公司强调的。要知道，2024年人们的注意力持续时间只有三秒钟。这确实令人悲哀，因为我们被各种通知、产品和信息狂轰滥炸。如果你不能在前三秒钟展示价值，用户就会流失。这也让我回想起你提到的联系人同步问题——用户必须注册，然后在第一晚就能在应用上看到所有好友并体验整个过程，否则就会流失用户。（01:27:55）：所以这种“倒置价值”的思路。在我与Dupe合作时，他们有一款购物应用，功能繁多。但我发现其中一个叫“Deal Hop”的功能很有趣——用户只需输入产品页面链接，应用就能找到该产品在网上的最低价。这正是我通过谷歌图片搜索、谷歌镜头等临时方法就能做到的事。我当时就想：“这应该能成就一家完整的公司。但如何教会用户使用这个功能，又如何以令人难忘的标志性方式尽快让他们获得‘啊哈时刻’呢？”（01:28:38）：我之前开发过一个产品，只需在现有网址前加上域名。我告诉他们：“你们应该试试这个功能。它很有市场潜力，但你们需要注册一个简洁且符合品牌定位的域名。”于是他花了不知道多少钱买下了Dupe.com。得知这个消息时我特别兴奋。心想，如果这个方法不成功，我会很难过，但如果成功了，那将是一次轰动性的成功。（01:29:05）：我们为此制作了几段视频，结果视频迅速走红，用户记住了在网址前加上dupe.com这个步骤。现在我觉得他们的ARR（年度经常性收入）已经破百万，而且上线不到60天。这就是一次轰动性的成功。在我合作的公司中，能取得如此显著成果的占50%，但大部分都以失败告终，因为用户需求实在难以预测。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so what I'm hearing is a big insight is just ideally get to three seconds time to value. Is that the advice?
turns.zh: 所以我听到的关键点是，要在三秒钟内让用户感受到价值。这就是你的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds great. Easy peasy.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。简单易行。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Yeah. You really have to craft onboarding everything to ensure that that's where the design part comes in of being a great product person.
turns.zh: 是的。你确实需要精心设计整个入门流程，这正是产品设计师发挥作用的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine a big part of this is just cutting things you think... Like killing your darlings, cutting things you think people need and just being really ruthless with that,.
turns.zh: 我觉得关键在于舍弃一些你认为必要的功能，比如“杀死心爱之物”，砍掉那些用户不需要的功能，必须足够果断。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Really ruthless, but also being extraordinarily creative with how you use the tools available to activate a user. I think extraordinary product people are deeply aware of every possible API and how it can be used in non-traditional ways. Like this URL trick was something that I think was non-traditional that people adopted very quickly. I have a whole laundry list of iOS mechanisms that people use for a certain way today, but you could invert them. (01:30:59): Contact sync is a great example because you sync your contacts and then it finds all the friends and then ranks the people who are not on the app yet but have a bunch of friends on it. So there's a bunch of ways that you can one tap, expose a ton of value to users that I think founders often neglect. A lot of founders will go and say, "Oh, they can just exchange usernames and that's how they can add each other." (01:31:27): That is the most unrealistic thing ever because that means you have to see the username, type it into the app. You have to do that what 50 times to get a 50-person friend list. So we're looking at 10,000 taps versus one. So that's what I mean by trying to get people to the activation moment, the aha moment and get them to value.
turns.zh: 真是无情啊，但你能以极具创造力的方式利用现有工具激活用户，这也确实令人惊叹。我认为优秀的产品人员深知每一种可能的API接口及其非传统使用方式。比如这个URL技巧，就是一个非传统但迅速被用户接受的创新思路。我能列举出一长串iOS机制，用户如今以某种方式在使用它们，但你完全可以反向思考这些机制。（01:30:59）：联系人同步就是一个绝佳例子。用户同步联系人后，系统会自动匹配所有好友，并对尚未下载该应用但好友众多的人进行排序。还有很多方法能一键触达用户价值，但很多创业者往往忽视了这一点。许多创业者会说：“用户可以直接交换用户名来添加好友。”（01:31:27）：这种想法太不现实了。用户得先看到用户名、手动输入应用，光是这样操作50次才能获得50个好友列表。而我们只需点击一次就能实现同样的效果。这就是我所说的引导用户触发激活时刻、实现“啊哈时刻”，让他们认识到产品价值的关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that advice. So maybe as just a last question along these lines. When you come to a founder, a relationship that you're a startup, you're trying to help, is there one more thing that you find often ends up being really helpful to them? Any common piece of advice that's like, "Oh, this is probably what's going to help you." You talked about this aha moment step, the contact sharing stuff. I guess is there anything else that's just like this is something that's probably going to help you with your app?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你的建议。最后再问一个相关问题。当你接触初创公司的创始人或合作伙伴时，比如帮助他们解决挑战，是否有某个常见建议对他们特别有用？比如“哦，这个方法很可能会帮助你”之类的。你提到的“啊哈时刻”步骤和联系人共享功能。还有其他可能对应用开发有帮助的要点吗？

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Right now, I think I advise around 35, 36 companies and all of them are at different stages of challenges they're facing. Some of them are pure at the product concept stage. Some of them are venture backed billion-dollar companies and each of them faces different problems. The first thing I often do is I ask them to show me the analytics. We look at how people are distributing the app today, what is the milestone that a user must hit to become activated and what's getting in the way of that? (01:33:03): I also take a very deep look at every funnel that users come through. And I think a lot of founders separate marketing and product growth, like top of funnel growth from the actual products growth mechanisms, but they're both the same. They both should be treated as the same. If you're targeting a community and you want them to all adopt and get saturation, you need to build marketing that shows imagery of that community or whatever. And then when you get in the app, you have to be able to join that community. (01:33:48): When you invite people from that app, that community needs to be mentioned. You need to actually cover everything from the ads to the in-app experience. All of that needs to be aligned for a user acquisition and flywheel to spin. A lot of people really screw that up. That's my initial rough approximation of what I do when I come in and try to fix or try to help with some of the challenges these companies are facing.
turns.zh: 目前，我为约35、36家公司提供咨询服务，他们所处的挑战阶段各不相同。有些还停留在产品概念阶段，有些是获得风险投资的亿级公司，每家公司都面临不同的问题。我首先会要求他们展示分析数据，观察用户当前的应用分发情况，用户必须达到的激活门槛，以及阻碍激活的障碍。（01:33:03）：我还会深入分析用户的每个转化路径。我发现许多创始人将市场营销和产品增长割裂开来，比如漏斗顶部的增长和实际产品增长机制，但两者本质相同，应该同等对待。如果你针对某个社区，想要让所有人采用并达到饱和，就需要打造能展现该社区形象的营销内容。而进入应用后，用户必须能融入这个社区。（01:33:48）：从应用中邀请用户时，必须提及这个社区。整个过程从广告到应用内体验都需要无缝衔接。所有这些环节必须协同，才能形成用户获取的良性循环。很多人在这方面做得很糟糕。这就是我介入后帮助解决这些挑战的大致思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is actually a great segue to the final thing I want to make sure people understand is you help companies through this. Talk about how you work with companies where they can find you, what kind of companies you're looking to work with and how all that works.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我想确保大家理解的一点是，你要帮助企业度过这个难关。谈谈你是如何与企业合作的，他们如何能找到你，你希望合作的企业类型，以及整个流程是怎样的。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: So I work across the gamut. Most of them are consumer mobile companies and there certainly are web ones too, but I work with companies across stages. Typically, I recommend that you don't book me unless you're venture backed because it's a little expensive. But my main goal when someone does seek my advice through intro is I try to make them 10 times back their money in the first 30 days. And so far I think I've managed to do that with anyone who's met with me. And that means get all the table stakes, grow things out of the way, at the minimum. (01:35:11): Then identify two to three step function changes that could change their growth trajectory. And these are higher scope fundamental changes to the product. So I try to couple both, explain to them which direction I believe they should go, and it's a conversation and we talk about it. And then once they settle on a direction, I tend to get in the pixels. I go into Figma and we do a live session together and clean things up. I identify, "Oh, that's going to convert at this percent." And then I just manage all that. But yeah, it's generally post-series A. (01:35:49): Some seed stage companies, and it's been really fun. It's kept my mind sharp on where the market is headed. I've also, over the years of building all these apps, I've accrued all these growth hacks that still nobody knows about. And so I share those when it's relevant for the company and it's been great. Dupe was one of them. I was advising Saturn. I rebuilt their Friend Finder. I think believe they're number one in the productivity section above ChatGPT as of today. But I think I've generally invested in about maybe 10% of the companies that seek out my advice.
turns.zh: 所以我的合作领域非常广泛。大多数客户是消费类移动应用公司，当然也有一些网页应用公司，但我与不同阶段的企业都有合作。通常，我建议除非是风投支持的公司，否则不接合作项目，因为费用有点高。但我的核心目标是，当有人通过介绍来寻求我的建议时，我会尽力让他们在前30天内获得10倍的投资回报。到目前为止，我认为我已经成功做到了。这意味着至少要解决基础问题，让业务顺利开展。（01:35:11）接下来，我会确定两到三个关键功能改进，以改变他们的增长轨迹。这些都是产品层面的重大变革。所以我会兼顾两方面，向他们说明我认为应该采取的方向，然后我们会进行讨论。一旦他们确定了方向，我就会深入细节。登录Figma平台，一起实时优化设计。我会指出：“哦，这个转化率会达到XX%。”然后我会全程跟进。是的，通常合作对象都是A轮之后的公司。（01:35:49）有些种子期公司合作也非常有趣。这让我对市场趋势保持敏锐。多年来开发这些应用，我积累了许多鲜为人知的增长技巧。当这些技巧与公司需求相关时，我会分享出来，效果很棒。比如Dupe项目，我为Saturn公司重建了Friend Finder功能。据我所知，截至目前，他们在生产力类别中已超越ChatGPT，位居榜首。但总体来说，我只投资了约10%寻求我建议的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Well, I know it feels expensive to some people, but if I were a company with cash, it feels like the best deal I could find someone like you to come in and actually help me think through deeply in the pixels how to make my thing work. So I think you're still undercharging and I hope you keep raising your prices because clearly there's a lot of demand. Nikita, this was incredible. I feel like people see you on Twitter and they're like, "Oh, this guy, he's such a jerk sometimes." But meeting you in person and talking to you, it's very clear. You're really a kind dude, really thoughtful. All your advice is based on real things you have done. It's not just you sitting around pontificating and I think that's incredibly valuable and I'm excited. People are tapping that knowledge and you're sharing it with people in a wider scale.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我知道对有些人来说价格偏高，但如果我是一家有资金的公司，找你这样的人来深入剖析如何让产品落地，我觉得是最划算的选择。所以我觉得你的收费还是太低了，希望你能提高收费标准，毕竟需求明显很大。尼基塔，你太棒了。我在推特上看到别人评价你：“哦，这家伙有时挺讨人厌的。”但亲自见面交流后，就能明显感受到你是个善良又深思熟虑的人。你所有的建议都基于真实经验，不只是纸上谈兵。这太有价值了，真为你感到兴奋。人们正在利用你的知识，而你也在更大范围内分享这些经验。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: It's been a pleasure. Thanks for having me. We covered a lot and there's plenty more. I hope to come back after the next viral hit.
turns.zh: 很荣幸能来参加这次访谈。我们聊了很多，还有更多内容想深入探讨。希望下次风靡全网的项目出来后能再来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. So I was going to ask you, is there anything you're working on now or stages, what can you share? [inaudible 01:37:33]. Stay tuned.
turns.zh: 天哪。所以我想问你，现在你在做什么项目，或者你能透露一些阶段性信息吗？[01:37:33的未录音内容]。敬请期待。

turns.speaker: Nikita Bier
turns.en: Stay tuned.
turns.zh: 敬请期待。

turns.en: Here we go. Amazing. I always ask people how can listeners be useful to you? So let me just ask you that as a final question, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 开始吧。太棒了。我总是问人们，听众如何能为你提供帮助？所以最后我想问你这个问题，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.en: Follow me on Twitter and enjoy my shit posts. And I hope you have as much fun as me on Twitter.
turns.zh: 欢迎在推特上关注我，欣赏我的那些沙雕动态。希望你们在推特上也能像我一样玩得开心。

turns.en: I do, man. I love your tweets. Nikita, thank you so much for doing this and for being here.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢，兄弟。我超爱你的推文。尼基塔，非常感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.en: Yeah, thanks a lot.
